docs.title: Software Delivery Needs a Harness, Not a Better Prompt
docs.text:
Let agents write the new parts of a deployment. Make the established rules executable so they do not have to guess them again.

An agent can write an Ansible role faster than I can. It can inspect a repository, find an entry point, draft a service unit, and propose the tasks needed to install it. That is useful. But what should happen when it has finished writing?

A green playbook is not the answer. A process can be active while its UI returns 500. A port can be open while the application is bound to the wrong address. A deployment can succeed once and reinstall the same files on every subsequent run.

In my earlier essay about engineer expectations, I argued that engineers now need to turn unclear needs into reliable systems of work, not merely turn requirements into code. Software delivery is a good place to test that claim. If an agent writes deployment code, the surrounding system must decide what counts as valid and what evidence counts as done.

The next step in agentic delivery is not to ask an LLM to make every operational decision. It is to build a harness around the work: a contract the agent can extend, deterministic tools that enforce decisions we have already made, and checks that can refuse a plausible but broken deployment.

By Rodrigo A. Diaz Leven — LinkedIn · GitHub · Resume

docs.title: What an agent has to guess when you say “install it”
docs.text:
Ask an agent: “Install OmniRoute for me.” Without a shared delivery contract, it has to fill in the blanks as it goes:

  1. Inspect the app. Is this a published release or a checkout that needs building? Does its native SQLite binding work on the target container's Node version?
  2. Choose a destination. Which host, container or VM, ports, and service account should it use? Those are operator decisions, not facts in the npm package.
  3. Write and run the install. It might choose latest, omit a required secret, or put a key in a command argument.
  4. Declare success. A running unit and an open port do not prove that the database works or that anonymous callers cannot spend the operator's provider credentials.

A harness changes that sequence. DeployFlow's example manifest includes a commented omniroute-release entry with the proxmox_lxc target and required secret names. Its release role pins and verifies the installed version, checks the native binding, and refuses anonymous inference requests that get through. The agent can draft changes to that role; the operator reviews them before appctl install omniroute-release runs. The role guide records what the checks mean and requires a second install with changed=0.

Do not spend model judgment on a decision you can encode and test. Save it for the application's unfamiliar behavior.

docs.title: Make the next deployment less dependent on memory
docs.text:
When a team learns that a service must render a page after a build, the finding should not live only in an incident note or in the engineer who restarted it. When it learns that a build needs a pinned source, that rule should not depend on whether the next prompt mentions it. In DeployFlow, the OmniRoute role now keeps both lessons: it checks the build receipt before shipping and requests /login after starting. The next agent need not know the original incident to encounter those checks.

Agents make it cheaper to write the next deployment. That increases the value of a system that can say no with a reason and yes with evidence.

I want agents to spend their time on the new questions: what this application is, what it needs, where the uncertain parts are, and which checks would prove that it works. I want Python, Ansible, tests, and the operator to handle the decisions we can already state precisely. Not because an LLM is incapable of making a good guess, but because a good guess is the wrong standard for a decision we have already made.

The best result is not an agent that can describe a successful deployment. It is a delivery system that can distinguish one from a convincing failure — and gets better each time that distinction proves inadequate.

docs.title: What belongs in the harness
docs.text:
I built DeployFlow to explore this approach. It is a working application-delivery repository, not an autonomous deployment agent. The current implementation uses Python for a small appctl command and Ansible to install and verify applications in target Proxmox LXC containers. A repository-local agent skill explains how to add an application. An operator reviews the changes and authorizes the install.

Each part gets the work it is good at:

  • The manifest records intent: which source, target, configuration, and secret names the application needs. A reviewer can inspect those choices before a run.
  • The LLM agent handles the unknowns: it investigates the app, asks the operator when a decision is missing, and drafts the manifest and app-specific role, following the add-app skill. It can coordinate that writing and review, but does not authorize its own deployment.
  • Python's appctl makes settled decisions deterministic: it parses and validates the manifest, rejects unsupported targets and missing secrets, and runs the agreed build and install sequence. It does not guess what an unknown target means.
  • Ansible roles declare and check desired state: they create or configure the target container, install files, start the service, and report changes. The application role checks whether this particular service actually works.
  • The operator owns the risk: a person reviews the diff and decides whether to run the install against the chosen host.

In the omniroute-release application, that sequence means:

  • Agent and operator: The agent investigates the release and proposes the manifest and role. The operator resolves unknowns, reviews the diff, and chooses whether to run the install.
  • appctl validates: Python checks the manifest and required secrets. Only proxmox_lxc is implemented; the target registry refuses target.kind: docker_vm before an install rather than silently treating it as an LXC.
  • Ansible applies and checks: The release role pins the npm version, verifies what was installed, starts the service, and checks its behavior. A successful command alone is not its definition of done.
  • The result comes back: appctl reports changes and checks to the operator. A repeat install should report changed=0 while the checks still run.

The same boundary handles other sources without making the agent guess a single install recipe: the source-built OmniRoute role requires a separate build and a commit receipt; the builder role provides an environment rather than a service port. The value is in making each decision explicit, then letting the right part of the workflow enforce it.

docs.title: A delivery workflow with an agent in it
docs.text:
The workflow begins before any remote command runs. An operator asks for an application. The agent reads the repository contract and add-app skill, asks about any missing choices, writes a manifest entry and an application role, and shows the diff. It does not silently choose production credentials or treat a guessed port as a requirement.

The operator reviews the choice of source, target, configuration, and checks. Then appctl validates what it can before mutation: it rejects unsupported target kinds, missing required secrets, and source/build mismatches. The Proxmox LXC target runs Ansible. The app role installs the artifact and tests the resulting service. A second install should report changed=0 and run the checks again.

Consider the Python example-app role. It is easy to tell the agent to write a task that starts the unit. It is more useful to require its role to assert that the package imports, the unit is active, the process listens on the configured address and port, and an endpoint answers. If the endpoint fails, the play must fail. Those are distinct claims. One does not follow from the other.

changed=0 is similarly narrow but valuable evidence. It says the same inputs did not require another install on a settled target container. It does not prove that no external dependency changed or that the app is healthy. That is why the application checks still run on the second pass. DeployFlow makes this visible in the example-app guide: run appctl install example-app again and the report should say 0 changed while the role still checks the package, unit, listener, and endpoint.

The agent can help write these checks. It cannot award itself a pass. Python validation and Ansible's observed results must make the final determination. That is what I mean by a tested agentic workflow: tests of the CLI contract, syntax checks for the playbook, a real install of worked examples, application-level postconditions, and a settled repeat run. It is not a claim that every new application or another person's infrastructure has already been tested.

This is also why a review of the generated diff remains necessary. A deterministic executor will reliably run a bad role. The harness reduces the number of decisions an agent must improvise; it does not remove the need to decide whether the role's application-specific checks are the right ones.

docs.title: The green deployment that returned 500
docs.text:
While installing the source-built OmniRoute instance, appctl streamed Ansible's tasks as they ran and saved log.txt, commands.txt, recap.txt, and errors.txt under tmp/runs/. The run showed that the new tree had shipped, Ansible had made changes, and the play had ended green. The service was active, its port was open, and /healthz returned 200. Yet the UI returned 500. Those records made the contradiction visible; they did not diagnose the page failure on their own.

The application's log supplied the missing clue: React could not find modules in its Client Manifest. The running process had loaded the old server bundle, while Ansible had replaced its files on disk. Restarting the service restored the UI.

A manual restart would not prevent the next failure. I updated the role to restart when the shipped bundle is newer than the process, then request /login. A 500 now fails the play even if /healthz returns 200. I also excluded Next.js's runtime route cache in the role defaults: rsync had been deleting that target-container cache, making every run look changed. Restarting on any transfer change would have caused needless restarts.

After a controlled stale-bundle test, appctl showed the restart and the subsequent installs reported 0 changed while checks still ran. The streamed run showed what Ansible did; the app log showed what it missed; the new page check made that lesson part of the next run.

docs.title: What the earlier tools already taught us
docs.text:
DeployFlow does not invent agent-assisted operations. That claim would ignore a useful body of prior work.

The kubectl-ai project shows an LLM helping users choose and call Kubernetes tools while Kubernetes performs the changes. The AWS deploy skill shows an agent inspecting an application, proposing cloud infrastructure, generating deployment code, and asking for confirmation. Appaloft and DaoFlow describe agent-facing delivery workflows for server or container targets. Ansible's AAP MCP service exposes existing automation to an external agent; that interface is not itself an LLM. Flux Operator's MCP tools likewise let a client ask for operations while a controller reconciles state.

These examples differ in targets and design. Their common lesson is more important than a feature checklist: an agent's ability to request a deployment is separate from the system's ability to apply and verify it. An MCP server is a tool interface, not proof of autonomous reasoning. An Ansible role is automation, not an agent. Human confirmation in a skill is a workflow rule, not an enforced approval protocol.

My narrower claim for DeployFlow is that it puts a reviewable application contract beside a tested Proxmox LXC and Ansible implementation. It couples the agent's drafting work to refusals and observable postconditions: a wrong source receipt, missing secret, unsupported target, failed endpoint, or repeat install that churns should be visible.

For example, the source-built OmniRoute role reads a build receipt and refuses to ship it if the recorded commit differs from the checkout's requested commit. The agent can propose a new role; that comparison still runs when the operator installs it. Some prior projects also offer contracts, verification, or target abstractions; the point is to make those properties real in this deployment path, not to claim they have never existed before.

That distinction protects an important question: what can a new user actually run? A successful deployment on my own host is evidence about that host. It is not a clean-clone acceptance test on a second Proxmox installation.

docs.title: Where judgment still belongs
docs.text:
Codifying known decisions does not settle every deployment decision. Someone still has to decide which application behavior matters, which failure should stop a release, how to handle data migration, what an acceptable outage is, and whether a credential has enough scope. Those choices depend on the service and its users.

Nor does an agent-facing skill make remote mutation safe by itself. A future interface that lets agents apply changes directly would need separate read, plan, and apply permissions; approval tied to the exact target, manifest, and artifact; scoped credentials; redacted audit evidence; and a tested account of retries and rollback. DeployFlow does not claim to provide that approval system today. The operator still controls when appctl install runs. In practice, an agent can follow the add-app skill to prepare a new role and show its diff; the operator decides whether to run the install against the configured Proxmox host. A skill's request for approval is not a technical substitute for that decision.

The harness can also fail. A postcondition can check the wrong endpoint. A lockfile can pin the wrong artifact. A health check can miss a broken UI. The answer is not to give the model wider authority; it is to improve the contract and the test when evidence exposes the miss. In the OmniRoute case, “process active” and “healthz 200” were true statements. They were insufficient statements.

That leads to a practical rule for teams building their own delivery workflows:

If the question is... Put the answer... What does this particular application need? In a reviewed manifest and app-specific role Which targets and input shapes are supported? In strict validation code How do we repeat the install? In a deterministic executor such as Ansible Did this service actually work? In observable application postconditions May this change reach this host now? With an accountable human or a tested approval mechanism

The table is not a demand for five layers of ceremony around a trivial script. It is a way to keep one kind of decision from being quietly delegated to the wrong component. Review depth should follow the risk of the deployment.

docs.title: builder
docs.text:
A guest whose purpose is to build other applications.

It installs no service and publishes no port. It assembles the environment a build needs — a compiler, a pinned Node, a workspace — and then stops. Nothing runs on it except the builds you send it.

This is a toolchain source. The other two kinds — package and repo — describe an application whose code comes from somewhere. This one's code comes from nowhere, because it is the environment.

docs.title: What is provisioned
docs.text: Guest builder, CT 123 CPU 6 cores RAM 24 GB Swap 4 GB Disk 60 GB Toolchain build-essential, git, ca-certificates, xz-utils, rsync Node 24.14.1, pinned and checksummed, at /opt/builder/node Workspace /var/lib/builder/work Service none Port none

docs.title: Install it
docs.text:
appctl install builder
appctl install builder        # must report changed=0

The manifest key is builder and the role directory is apps/builder/. They have to match: appctl install selects the role with --tags lxc,<key>, and a key that is not a role name selects nothing. The play runs, changes nothing, and reports success.

docs.title: Why 24 GB
docs.text:
Measured, not guessed. The build's webpack process caps its heap at 10 GB (NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=10240) and reaches about 11.5 GB RSS before it finishes.

A 12 GB builder was tried first. It failed in a way that named nothing useful: the build spun with 96 MB free and 348 MB available, the guest stopped answering SSH entirely, and pct exec returned

lxc-attach: 123: ../src/lxc/attach.c: lxc_attach: 1615
Cannot allocate memory - Failed to clone attached process

The play that launched the build was green. The failure looked like a network timeout.

The role asserts the floor, so a builder that is resized by hand is checked at install time rather than discovered during a build.

docs.title: How a build finds it
docs.text:
Guest hostnames do not resolve from the controller — Proxmox registers the hostname in its own resolver, and the controller is not on that side of the network. The address has to be discovered.

common/lxc already does that: it reads the lease with pct exec <vmid> -- hostname -I and sets ansible_host from it. The builder role writes the same address to a file the build script can read:

tmp/builders/builder.endpoint

host=10.0.0.80
user=root
node_dir=/opt/builder/node
work=/var/lib/builder/work

The file lives under tmp/, which is gitignored, because it is a runtime artifact: the address is a DHCP lease and changes when the guest is rebuilt. It is rewritten by every play, so it is never stale.

user is part of the file on purpose. A script that reads host and leaves the user out gets $USER from ssh — which is not root on the controller — and the connection fails with "Too many authentication failures". That error looks like a credential problem and is not one.

docs.title: What the role asserts
docs.text:
Every assertion is about the machine, not about an install. A role that installs a compiler and reports success has not said anything about whether a build can run on it.

Assertion What it catches uname -m is x86_64 a builder under emulation, where esbuild's Go runtime faults Node reports the pinned version a runtime the tree was not built against npm-cli.js exists a Node tarball that is not a Node tarball ≥ 24 GB of RAM a guest that thrashes during the build ≥ 6 cores a guest too slow to be worth having ≥ 40 GB free on the workspace a build that fails on "No space left on device" registry.npmjs.org reachable a build that fails at npm ci with a network error

docs.title: Why it does not depend on common/python
docs.text:
common/python asserts that app_port is defined. A builder serves nothing, so it has no port, and the assertion would fail on a guest that is otherwise correct.

apps/builder/meta/main.yml declares dependencies: [] on purpose. A role with no dependency still runs — play 2 of playbooks/site.yml loops over each host's app_roles and include_roles it — so nothing in the playbook changes.

The consequence: a builder gets none of the framework's app_home, app_dir or app_venv variables, and none of the recursive chown in the play's post_tasks. It defines what it needs.

docs.title: The runtime is pinned in one place
docs.text:
Node's version and checksum live in apps/builder/defaults/main.yml:

builder_node_version: 24.14.1
builder_node_sha256: 84d38715d449447117d05c3e71acd78daa49d5b1bfa8aacf610303920c3322be

The build script does not install a runtime. It asserts the builder has one and fails with a named error if it does not:

FATAL: no pinned Node at /opt/builder/node

That is the difference between an environment that is provisioned and one that is whatever apt-get returned on the day.

docs.title: npm is invoked through its JS entry
docs.text:
/opt/builder/node/bin/npm is a symlink to npm-cli.js, and that file starts with #!/usr/bin/env node. Nothing under /opt is on PATH on a stock guest, so the shim dies:

env: 'node': No such file or directory

Invoke the interpreter by absolute path and the entry script by path:

NPM_CLI="$NODE_DIR/lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npm-cli.js"
node "$NPM_CLI" ci --no-audit --no-fund

docs.title: Where it is used
docs.text: apps/omniroute builds OmniRoute on this guest. The full story — including why the build cannot run on the controller — is in ../omniroute/docs/BUILDING-FROM-SOURCE.md.

docs.title: example-app
docs.text:
The sample application used by the quickstart. It installs in one command and needs nothing but a Proxmox host:

appctl install example-app

It exists to show what an application role owes the framework, and to be genuinely runnable — the checks below are the point, and they are the checks every other role in this repository is modelled on.

An application role is one directory with four obligations:

  1. defaults/main.yml names the application, its port, the package it installs and the module it serves. Everything else is derived from app_name.
  2. meta/main.yml declares the dependency on common/python, so adding an application never edits a playbook.
  3. tasks/main.yml installs the application and then proves it works.
  4. files/ holds the pinned lockfile and the module the server imports.

The third is the one that matters. The checks in this role cover the failures a green play hides: a package tree that did not install, a module that cannot be imported, a service that is up but bound to the wrong port, and a service that answers nothing.

docs.title: Three things this role gets right that are easy to get wrong
docs.text:
The lockfile is copied to the guest. pip runs on the guest, and pip on the guest cannot open a path on the controller. Pointing pip at the controller's path fails with "Could not open requirements file" — which names a missing file rather than a file that is present, on a different machine. So the file travels first, and pip is pointed at where it landed.

The import check uses a module name, not the application name. example-app contains a hyphen and is not a valid Python identifier, so import example-app is a syntax error rather than a missing module — and the check would fail for a reason that has nothing to do with the install. The module is example_app, and the unit's PYTHONPATH points at the install root where it lives.

The role checks the manifest's pin. The manifest says package: "bottle==0.13.3" and this role installs bottle==0.13.3. Those are two files, and they can drift. The role refuses to run when they disagree, because a mismatch means the role would install something other than what the operator reviewed.

docs.title: Replace it with your own application, and keep the checks.
docs.text: See .agents/skills/deployflow-add-app/SKILL.md for the contract a role follows, and the repository README for the workflow as a whole.

docs.title: Building OmniRoute from source
docs.text:
What it takes to build cheaper-inference/OmniRoute at main into an artifact that runs on an x86_64 Linux guest, and what fails on the way there.

This is written from the measurements, not from the theory. Every failure listed here happened, and the symptom is what was actually observed — not what would be expected.

docs.title: The shape of the problem
docs.text:
Controller arm64 macOS (Apple Silicon), 48 GB Guest x86_64 Linux, Proxmox LXC Upstream cheaper-inference/OmniRoute, branch main, version 3.8.52 Commit built edab7c3a59bf7d6f040d581dbda3a46adbee0d57 Runtime Node >=22.22.2 <23 \|\| >=24.0.0 <27 — pinned to 24.14.1 Build recipe npm run build:release

The controller and the guest are different architectures. That single fact causes every hard problem below.

docs.title: The platform mismatch, and why it is slow to find
docs.text:
A tree built on arm64 macOS carries darwin-only native binaries:

  • sharp-darwin-arm64
  • @esbuild/darwin-arm64
  • lightningcss-darwin-arm64

The guest needs sharp-linux-x64 and friends.

better-sqlite3 hides the problem. It ships a prebuild for every platform, so it loads on the guest even from a macOS build, and the tree gets all the way to serving requests before sharp fails deep in a request handler. Checking better-sqlite3 alone would have said "the tree is fine".

The check that actually catches it is a write through the native binding, not a load:

const db = new Database(":memory:");
db.exec("CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER)");
db.prepare("INSERT INTO t VALUES (?)").run(42);

docs.title: Where the build can run, and where it cannot
docs.text: Three options were tried. Two failed, and they failed for different reasons.

docs.title: 1. Native build on the controller — wrong architecture
docs.text: Worked. Produced a dist/server.js that ran locally. Useless for the guest: the natives are darwin.

docs.title: 2. Container on the controller, emulated — failed twice
docs.text:
docker run --platform linux/amd64 on the arm64 host. The architecture is right and then two separate things go wrong.

Failure A — out of memory. The Next.js webpack build needs roughly 10 GB. The emulated process sees the VM's memory, not the container's limit, and is SIGKILLed at about 5.6 GB:

Next.js build worker exited with code: null and signal: SIGKILL

Raising the Colima VM from 8 GB to 20 GB fixes this one. The build then proceeds normally and generates all 637 static pages.

Failure B — the Go runtime faults under qemu. esbuild is a Go binary. Under qemu its runtime dies:

fatal error: receive on synctest channel from outside bubble

goroutine 3 [running]:
main.(*serviceType).sendRequest(...)
    github.com/evanw/esbuild/cmd/esbuild/service.go:192 +0x12b
...
Next.js build worker exited with code: null and signal: SIGSEGV

This is not a memory problem and no amount of memory fixes it. Emulation is simply not reliable for this build.

A third, smaller failure in the same image: node:24-bookworm-slim has gcc but no g++ or make. better-sqlite3 is an optional dependency that compiles a native binding on install; with no toolchain its install script fails, npm treats the optional dependency as skippable, and it is silently absent from the tree. The application then falls back to another driver or fails at the first query, and nothing says the binding is missing.

docs.title: 3. Native build on an x86_64 host — works
docs.text:
The Proxmox node is x86_64: the guest's exact platform. 12 CPUs, 125 GB RAM, 96 GB free.

emulated container native x86_64 npm ci 8 min 1 min webpack build SIGSEGV 637 pages, 17 s esbuild Go runtime fault works

The build runs there as itself. No emulation, no cross-compilation.

docs.title: The build host is a guest this repository provisions
docs.text:
The first version of this build used the Proxmox node itself as the build host, because it was already there and already x86_64. That works, and it is the wrong shape: the node is shared infrastructure, and a build that reaches 11.5 GB of RSS and writes 16 GB to /root is a build that can take the node with it.

So the build host is now a guest — CT 123, builder — provisioned by this repository like any other application. It is created by appctl install builder and it installs no service: it is a toolchain, an application whose purpose is to be the environment another application is built in.

appctl install builder        # creates CT 123, installs the toolchain
sh apps/omniroute/build/omr-build-linux.sh   /Users/bruj0/Projects/Omniroute main

docs.title: How the build finds it
docs.text:
Guest hostnames do not resolve from the controller. Proxmox registers the hostname in its own resolver, and the controller is not on that side of the network — ansible -i inventory/hosts.yml builder -m stat fails with "Could not resolve hostname builder". The address has to be discovered, and common/lxc already does that: it reads the lease with pct exec <vmid> -- hostname -I and sets ansible_host from it.

The build script needs the same address, and it is not the ansible controller. So the builder role publishes it to a file both sides can read:

tmp/builders/builder.endpoint

host=10.0.0.80
user=root
node_dir=/opt/builder/node
work=/var/lib/builder/work

The file lives under tmp/, which is gitignored, because it is a runtime artifact: the address is a DHCP lease and changes when the guest is rebuilt. It is rewritten by every play, so it is never stale.

The user is part of the address, not an argument. The build script reads user from the same file and builds root@10.0.0.80 from it. Left out, ssh defaults to $USER — which on this controller is not root — and the connection fails with "Too many authentication failures" after the agent offers five keys against an authorized_keys that holds one. That is a confusing error for a credential problem that is not really a credential problem.

docs.title: The toolchain is asserted, not assumed
docs.text:
The builder role installs build-essential, git, ca-certificates, xz-utils and rsync, and a pinned Node 24.14.1 fetched with a checksum. It then asserts the properties a build depends on:

Assertion What it catches uname -m is x86_64 a builder running under emulation, where esbuild's Go runtime faults Node reports the pinned version a runtime the tree was not built against npm-cli.js exists a Node tarball that is not a Node tarball ≥ 24 GB of RAM a guest that thrashes during the build (see below) ≥ 6 cores a guest that builds too slowly to be worth having ≥ 40 GB free on the workspace a build that fails on "No space left on device" registry.npmjs.org reachable a build that fails at npm ci with a network error

Each of these is a result, not an exit code. A role that installs a compiler and reports success has not said anything about whether a build can run on it.

docs.title: 12 GB was not enough, and the failure was silent
docs.text:
The first builder was created with 12 GB of RAM — 10 GB of heap cap plus 2 GB of headroom, which sounds right on paper. It was not.

The build's webpack process reaches about 11.5 GB RSS against that 10 GB heap cap. On a 12 GB guest the arithmetic leaves nothing: the build was observed spinning with 96 MB free and 348 MB available, and then the guest stopped answering SSH entirely. The banner timed out. pct exec returned:

lxc-attach: 123: ../src/lxc/attach.c: lxc_attach: 1615
Cannot allocate memory - Failed to clone attached process

Even the Proxmox host could not get a shell into the container, because cloning a process inside the container needs memory the container does not have.

Nothing in the build's own output said "out of memory". The play that launched it was green. The failure looked like a network problem — a connection timeout — and it was a memory problem, three layers down.

24 GB clears it. The build then runs with 21 GB available and a peak RSS of 2.7 GB in the observed sample, with the page cache holding the rest. The role asserts the floor, so a builder resized by hand is checked at install time rather than discovered during a build.

This is the lesson the framework already had, restated at a new scale: a guest that is too small does not fail at install, it fails hours later with an error that names a memory limit rather than the guest.

docs.title: The clone is pinned to a commit, not to a branch
docs.text:
The build host clones the repository itself (see the next section for why), and the first version of the script cloned --branch main. main moves: a push between the controller reading HEAD and the builder cloning produces an artifact built from a commit the receipt does not name.

The receipt is the role's provenance check — the role refuses a tree whose receipt does not match the checkout's HEAD — so a receipt that is wrong defeats the check it exists to satisfy. The clone is now pinned:

git clone --branch "$REF" "$REPO_URL" "$BUILD_DIR"
git -C "$BUILD_DIR" fetch --quiet origin "$COMMIT"
git -C "$BUILD_DIR" checkout --quiet --detach "$COMMIT"
test "$(git -C "$BUILD_DIR" rev-parse HEAD)" = "$COMMIT"

The explicit fetch is needed because a shallow branch clone may not contain the commit once the branch has moved past it, and the final test is there so the build fails rather than shipping an artifact from the wrong commit.

docs.title: The toolchain lives on the builder, not in the build script
docs.text:
The remote build script used to install its own toolchain: apt-get install build-essential, download Node, unpack it. Now it asserts that the builder has them and fails with a named error if it does not.

That is a better shape for three reasons. The build is reproducible because the environment is provisioned and checksummed by a role, not by whatever apt-get returned on the day. The builder's Node is pinned and checksummed in one place — apps/builder/defaults/main.yml — instead of two copies that can drift. And the build script's failure message can name the actual cause, because the check is a check and not an installation:

FATAL: no compiler on this build host
       the builder role installs build-essential; this host is not it

docs.title: npm is invoked through its JS entry, not its bin shim
docs.text:
/opt/builder/node/bin/npm is a symlink to npm-cli.js, and that file starts with #!/usr/bin/env node. Nothing under /opt is on PATH on a stock guest, so the shim dies:

env: 'node': No such file or directory

The build invokes the interpreter by absolute path and the entry script by path:

NPM_CLI="$NODE_DIR/lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npm-cli.js"
node "$NPM_CLI" ci --no-audit --no-fund

This is the same trap the skill already records for the OpenAI CLI shims, and it is worth stating again because it is a failure with no useful message: the shell reports a missing node when the problem is that node exists and is not on the PATH.

docs.title: What the build host needs, and why a clone rather than a transfer
docs.text:
Two independent reasons, both measured.

The sha has to resolve. build:release runs OMNIROUTE_BUILD_SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD). A transferred tree has no .git, so the sha is empty and the artifact carries no provenance at all — dist/BUILD_SHA is written empty and the receipt has nothing to record.

A tar of the controller's checkout carries macOS sidecars. Every file on an APFS volume may have a ._name AppleDouble companion. They survive tar, and esbuild reads them as source files:

src/mitm/._aliasConfig.ts:1:0: ERROR: Unexpected "\x00"
src/mitm/._childExitCleanup.ts:1:0: ERROR: Unexpected "\x00"
...
Error: Build failed with 77 errors

So the build host runs git clone itself. The repository is public, so it needs no credential. A private one needs a token the host already holds.

docs.title: The dependency tree is not a graph you can walk
docs.text:
The server runs from dist/ alone. Verified by moving the root node_modules away and starting it — it served, bound its ports, and shut down cleanly. dist/ carries its own node_modules (741 MB) and its own .build/next (312 MB).

The CLI is different. It needs packages that are not in dist/node_modules. The first attempt computed their closure by scanning the CLI's imports. That is fragile in three separate ways, and each one only surfaced on the guest:

What the scan missed Symptom on the guest await import("tsx/esm") — a dynamic import Cannot find package 'tsx' imported from .../bin/omniroute.mjs the loader resolves from src/ and open-sse/, not just bin/ Cannot find package 'ws' imported from .../open-sse/utils/setupPolyfill.ts @esbuild/linux-x64 is an optional dependency, chosen by an install script that reads os and cpu The package "@esbuild/linux-x64" could not be found, and is needed by esbuild

The third one is the reason a dependency walk can never be complete: npm installs those packages by running a script that inspects the current platform, not by resolving a graph. No graph walk reaches them.

So the tree npm ci produced is shipped as-is. It is correct by construction. The cost is a 1.2 GB transfer that takes seconds on a LAN.

The CLI's own diagnostic is the check that it is right:

Summary: 7 ok, 43 warning(s), 0 failure(s)

The 43 warnings are absent optional provider CLIs (claude, codex, gemini and friends). Zero failures is the signal.

docs.title: What the artifact is
docs.text:
dist/            1.0 GB   the server bundle, with its own .build/next
bin/             the CLI
node_modules/    the dependency tree, native linux-x64

The root .build/ is 5.4 GB of webpack cache and does not travel. The build has already produced the 312 MB dist/.build/next that the runtime reads.

The root node_modules is 4.3 GB unpacked but tarballs to 1.2 GB.

docs.title: Pinning the runtime
docs.text:
The engines field allows a range, and a runtime outside it fails at import rather than at install:

{"node": ">=22.22.2 <23 || >=24.0.0 <27"}

The tree is built with one Node and must run on one. Node 24.14.1 is pinned and checksummed against the sha256 nodejs.org publishes in its SHASUMS256.txt.

npm's own bin shim runs #!/usr/bin/env node, and nothing under app_home is on PATH on a stock guest, so it dies with env: 'node': No such file or directory before the application starts. The interpreter is therefore named by path, and the operator-facing command is a wrapper rather than a symlink to the package's own bin entry.

docs.title: The receipt is what makes changed=0 possible
docs.text:
The build writes .deployflow-build.json into the checkout:

{
  "commit": "edab7c3a59bf7d6f040d581dbda3a46adbee0d57",
  "shortCommit": "edab7c3a59",
  "version": "3.8.52",
  "ref": "main",
  "platform": "linux-amd64",
  "node": "24",
  "builtAt": "2026-10-24T16:30:24Z"
}

The role compares the commit in the receipt against the checkout's HEAD and refuses a tree that does not match. Without it the role has nothing to compare, and either reinstalls every time or trusts an mtime.

The role never builds. A role that rebuilds on every play cannot tell "no changes" from "rebuilt".

docs.title: The rsync flags that are load-bearing
docs.text:
The tree is shipped with ansible.posix.synchronize. Two flags are not optional, and each failure is silent:

  • --links — without it a symlinked node_modules arrives with its packages but empty subdirectories, and every entry point fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND for a package that is present.
  • --times — without it synchronize's own --delay-updates staging renames every file at the end of the run, giving it a fresh mtime. The next run sees the whole tree as different, transfers all of it again, and reports changed forever.

Two flags have to be absent, and both were found the hard way:

  • --chown — the controller is macOS, whose rsync is openrsync, a compatible reimplementation that does not implement it: 

    rsync: unrecognized option `--chown=omniroute:omniroute'
    The task fails outright. Ownership is set on the guest by a separate task instead, which works the same on every controller.

  • --owner --group — these make rsync set each file's owner to the controller's uid, which is 501 on macOS and nobody on the guest. The chown task then sets it back, and the next run repeats both. The role reported changed=2 forever on a tree that had not changed. Without them, rsync leaves the ownership of existing files alone and the second run is changed=0.

docs.title: The postconditions that matter
docs.text:
Assert Guards against dist/server.js is on the guest a transfer that stopped half way better-sqlite3 loads and takes a write a native module built for the wrong platform omniroute doctor is healthy the application's own opinion of itself storage.sqlite exists and is not empty a running server with nothing to log in to the listener is on the configured address the process listening somewhere else /healthz answers 200 a service that binds a port and does not serve /v1/chat/completions answers 401 without a key an inference plane any device can spend /v1 answers 401 for a bad key, and names the gate a proxy answering 401 instead of the application /api/providers answers 401 a dashboard serving an anonymous caller the unit is enabled a service that does not come back after a reboot

The key gate checks are the ones worth reading. A server that serves /v1 without a key spends the operator's provider credentials for anyone who can reach the port, and nothing else in the play would notice.

docs.title: Measured results
docs.text: Build on the builder guest 28 min end to end, including the transfer npm ci 1 min (8 min emulated) Transfer to the guest ~50 s for 3.9 GB over rsync with compression First install 80 tasks, 2 changed Second install 80 tasks, 0 changed Build host CT 123, builder, 10.0.0.80, 6 cores / 24 GB / 60 GB Runtime guest CT 122, omniroute-src, 10.0.0.78 Served version 3.8.52, BUILD_SHA=edab7c3a59

docs.title: Reproducing it
docs.text:
appctl install builder        # the build host; CT 123

apps/omniroute/build/omr-build-linux.sh \
  /Users/bruj0/Projects/Omniroute main

appctl install omniroute
appctl install omniroute      # must be changed=0

The build script takes the checkout and the ref. It finds the build host itself, by reading tmp/builders/builder.endpoint — the file the builder role writes. There is no host argument, because a guest address is a DHCP lease and a host argument would be a value that goes stale.

docs.title: omniroute-release
docs.text:
OmniRoute, installed from a published npm release, served by one systemd unit on one guest.

This is the release shape. The other OmniRoute role in this repository (apps/omniroute/) builds a tree from a source checkout on a build guest; this one installs a released artifact that npm publishes, and the guest's own npm install does the work. Nothing OmniRoute-related runs on the controller except the install itself.

docs.title: What is deployed
docs.text: Guest omniroute, CT 120 Release omniroute@3.8.51 from npm, pinned Runtime Node 24.14.1, pinned and checksummed, under app_home/node Unit omniroute.service Port 20128 — dashboard, /v1 proxy, MCP/A2A and management API together Port 20132 — the realtime dashboard WebSocket, published to match State /opt/omniroute/state, never touched by a reinstall Install root /opt/omniroute/app/npm, beside the inert Python venv Secrets five, all generated, none ever in argv

docs.title: Install it
docs.text:
appctl install omniroute-release
appctl install omniroute-release        # must report changed=0

The manifest key is omniroute-release and the role directory is apps/omniroute-release/. They have to match: appctl install selects the role with --tags lxc,<key>, and a key that is not a role name selects nothing.

docs.title: Why its secrets are named omniroute_release_*
docs.text:
Two guests run this application: this role installs the published release, and apps/omniroute/ builds one from a checkout. Both derive their paths from app_name, so both write /opt/omniroute and both read a credentials file with the same five keys.

One .env cannot hold two storage encryption keys. The release role's credentials are therefore named omniroute_release_*, and the source-built role keeps the unscoped names. Two guests, two key sets, one file.

The cost is a name that repeats the role, and the benefit is that adopting a guest under this role cannot rotate a key the other guest is using. The storage encryption key and storage.sqlite are one backup set: a rotated key leaves every stored provider credential undecryptable.

docs.title: Why the role is named omniroute-release but the app is omniroute
docs.text:
Two roles cannot share a name, and apps/omniroute/ already owns the first one. So the role directory is omniroute-release.

The guest side is a different question, and the answer is app_name: omniroute. Everything the framework derives comes from app_name:

Derived from app_name Value app_user omniroute app_home /opt/omniroute app_dir /opt/omniroute/app app_state_dir /opt/omniroute/state app_service_name omniroute

A second name would mean a second service account, a second install root and a second state directory — and the state directory is where the stored provider keys, the encrypted credential table and the conversation history live. A second name would be a working service with an empty database.

So the role name and app_name differ on purpose. The role name is what the inventory and appctl refer to; app_name is what the guest sees.

docs.title: The credentials file is group-readable, on purpose
docs.text:
The credentials live in state/secrets/env, owned by root with group app_user and mode 0640. The service account can read it and cannot write it.

That is not a weakening. The file stays root-owned and unwritable by the process it belongs to, so a compromised application cannot rewrite the key that encrypts its own store. What it does have to do is read it, because the operator wrapper in /usr/local/bin/omniroute loads it and exports what it finds.

The failure this prevents was measured on CT 120. With the file at 0600 and group root:

FAIL Storage/encryption: Encrypted credentials exist but STORAGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY is missing

The server was perfectly healthy throughout. It had the key, because systemd reads the EnvironmentFile as PID 1 before it drops privileges. The doctor diagnostic did not, because it runs through the wrapper as the service account — and the wrapper could not open a root-only file. The role failed on a guest whose service was fine.

The same applies to the directory holding it: root:app_user at 0750, so the service account can traverse into it.

docs.title: What the role refuses
docs.text:
Each of these is a failure a green play would otherwise hide:

Check Catches the credentials are non-empty a secret that was never set, before a 546 MB download the password is at least 8 characters omniroute setup rejecting it later, against a one-time bootstrap no credential contains a newline a value silently truncated by the EnvironmentFile format the pinned Node is on disk a runtime outside the range OmniRoute accepts npm is 11 or later --allow-scripts being rejected mid-install the installed version is the pinned one a release someone bumped by hand the package .env is gone a file inside the install root that a version bump replaces the embedding library is writable the memory subsystem silently degraded to FTS5-only the native SQLite binding loads a server running on the WASM fallback with WAL disabled the store exists and is non-empty a running server with nothing to log in to the store is in WAL mode a driver that cannot do write-ahead logging the listeners are on the configured address "the service is on the LAN" versus "the variables say it should be" an anonymous /v1 call is refused an inference plane any device on the network can spend an invalid key is refused the key gate being off, which lets invalid keys through as anonymous traffic an anonymous /api call is refused a dashboard with no administrator password the unit is enabled a service that comes back stopped after a reboot

The last three are the ones worth reading. They run from the controller against the guest's LAN address, because the question they answer is what a peer on the network can reach — and inside the guest the same request can be answered differently.

docs.title: The version pin
docs.text:
omr_version is pinned to an exact version, never latest. A floating tag makes two plays of the same role install different code, which is the opposite of what a pinned role is for.

The role compares the installed version by asking the release itself (omniroute --version), not by reading a stamp file. A stamp can disagree with the directory it describes — a half-finished install, a directory left behind by an interrupted play — and then every task that trusts it skips the install that would have repaired it.

docs.title: The compile toolchain is off
docs.text:
omr_install_build_toolchain: false. better-sqlite3 ships a prebuild for linux-x64 at this Node, so a compiling guest is the exception rather than the rule.

When a version bump outruns the prebuild, the role does not silently carry a C++ compiler on every guest: it fails at the binding assertion and names the remedy — either rebuild the binding in place, or set omr_install_build_toolchain: true and re-run.

docs.title: Why the secrets never reach argv
docs.text:
omniroute setup --non-interactive reads INITIAL_PASSWORD from the environment. The wrapper takes it from the root-owned credentials file, so the password is never a command-line argument — and ps on the guest is world-readable.

The bootstrap runs once. It is gated on a marker in the state tree, so a reinstall does not re-apply it and lock the operator out. The marker is never written over a failure: a marker written over a failure is the one thing that would make the next play skip the task that has to be retried.

docs.title: Source
docs.text: This role was migrated from the omniroute application in the proxmox-lxc-ansible repository, which is where the release shape was originally written and where CT 120 was first provisioned.

docs.title: omniroute
docs.text:
OmniRoute, built from a source checkout, served by one systemd unit on one guest. Nothing OmniRoute-related runs on the controller except the build: no checkout is read during the play except to check a receipt, and no bundle is produced there.

This is the from-source shape. The published-release shape — one pinned npm version, npm install fetches it — is a different role and is not this one.

This application works. It is not a sample: it deploys, it verifies, and a second install reports changed=0. It is also the harder of the two shipped shapes, because it is the one an agent is most likely to get wrong — the build cannot run where the agent is, and the role has to refuse a stale tree rather than rebuild one.

docs.title: What is deployed
docs.text: Guest omniroute-src, CT 122 Source cheaper-inference/OmniRoute at main, resolved to a commit Build Linux amd64, on the builder guest — never on the controller, never emulated Runtime Node 24.14.1, pinned and checksummed, under app_home/node Unit omniroute.service Port 20128 — dashboard, /v1 proxy, MCP/A2A and management API together Port 20132 — the realtime dashboard WebSocket, published to match State /opt/omniroute/state, never touched by a reinstall Install root /opt/omniroute/app/src, beside the inert Python venv Secrets five, all generated, none ever in argv

docs.title: Why the build runs on its own guest
docs.text:
The controller is arm64 macOS. The guest is x86_64 Linux. A tree built on the controller carries darwin-only native binaries — sharp-darwin-arm64, @esbuild/darwin-arm64, lightningcss-darwin-arm64 — and the guest's Linux builds need sharp-linux-x64.

better-sqlite3 hides this: it ships a prebuild for every platform, so it loads on the guest even from a macOS build. sharp and esbuild do not, and they fail much later as an unrelated error deep in a request handler.

So the build runs on a native x86_64 build host. That host is a guest this repository provisions for the purpose: apps/builder/, a toolchain application with 6 cores, 24 GB of RAM and a pinned Node.

appctl install builder        # the build host; CT 123

apps/omniroute/build/omr-build-linux.sh \
  /Users/bruj0/Projects/Omniroute main

The build script finds the host itself, by reading tmp/builders/builder.endpoint — the file the builder role writes. There is no host argument: a guest address is a DHCP lease and a host argument would be a value that goes stale.

The settings match the project's own CI recipe (.github/workflows/build.yml): ONNXRUNTIME_NODE_INSTALL=skip, OMNIROUTE_USE_TURBOPACK=0, and a 10 GB heap cap.

docs.title: Why not a container on the controller
docs.text:
A container with --platform linux/amd64 on an arm64 host gets the architecture right and then falls over, in two separate ways:

Failure Cause Next.js build worker exited with code: null and signal: SIGKILL at ~5.6 GB the emulated process sees the VM's memory, not the container's limit. Raising the VM to 20 GB fixes this one. fatal error: receive on synctest channel from outside bubble / SIGSEGV esbuild is a Go binary, and the Go runtime faults under qemu. No amount of memory fixes this.

The second one is the real reason. Emulation is not reliable for this build, so the build host is native.

It was the Proxmox node at first, because that machine was already x86_64 and already there. That is the wrong shape: the node is shared infrastructure, and a build that reaches 11.5 GB of RSS and writes 16 GB to /root is a build that can take the node with it. So the build host is a guest now, provisioned like any other application.

docs.title: Why the build host clones the repository
docs.text:
The build host runs git clone itself rather than receiving a transferred tree, for two measured reasons:

  • git rev-parse --short HEAD has to resolve. The build reads the sha from git, and a transferred tree has no .git, so the artifact carries no provenance at all.
  • A tar of the controller's checkout carries macOS AppleDouble sidecars (._aliasConfig.ts and hundreds like it). esbuild reads them as source files and the build fails with 77 errors: src/mitm/._aliasConfig.ts:1:0: ERROR: Unexpected "\x00".

And it clones a commit, not a branch. git clone --branch main resolves main at clone time, and main moves: a push between the controller reading HEAD and the builder cloning produces an artifact built from a commit the receipt does not name — which defeats the provenance check the receipt exists to satisfy.

git clone --branch "$REF" "$REPO_URL" "$BUILD_DIR"
git -C "$BUILD_DIR" fetch --quiet origin "$COMMIT"
git -C "$BUILD_DIR" checkout --quiet --detach "$COMMIT"
test "$(git -C "$BUILD_DIR" rev-parse HEAD)" = "$COMMIT"

The explicit fetch is needed because a shallow branch clone may not contain the commit once the branch has moved past it, and the final test is there so a wrong commit fails the build rather than shipping.

docs.title: Why the dependency tree is not reconstructed
docs.text:
The CLI's dependency closure was first computed by walking the CLI's imports. That is fragile in three ways, and each one only showed up on the guest:

Miss Symptom on the guest await import("tsx/esm") — a dynamic import Cannot find package 'tsx' the loader resolves from src/ and open-sse/, not just bin/ Cannot find package 'ws' @esbuild/linux-x64 is an optional dependency chosen by an install script The package "@esbuild/linux-x64" could not be found, and is needed by esbuild

So the tree npm ci produced is shipped as-is. It is correct by construction.

docs.title: The receipt
docs.text:
The build writes .deployflow-build.json into the checkout:

{
  "commit": "edab7c3a59bf7d6f040d581dbda3a46adbee0d57",
  "shortCommit": "edab7c3a59",
  "version": "3.8.52",
  "ref": "main",
  "platform": "linux-amd64",
  "node": "24",
  "builtAt": "2026-10-24T15:35:29Z"
}

The role reads it and refuses to ship a tree whose commit is not the commit in the checkout. This is what makes the second run reach changed=0: without a receipt the role has nothing to compare and either reinstalls every time or trusts an mtime.

The role never builds. A role that rebuilds on every play cannot tell "no changes" from "rebuilt". The build is an operator act, and the role's job is to refuse.

docs.title: What the role refuses
docs.text:
Each of these is a refusal with a message that names what to do, not a warning:

Refusal Why no checkout on the controller the role ships a tree, it does not fetch one the checkout is not on the requested ref two plays that both build main produce two different artifacts the receipt names a different commit the tree is not the one that was asked for dist/server.js does not exist a checkout without a build looks exactly like a build that failed the tree did not arrive on the guest the transfer is the part most likely to fail quietly better-sqlite3 does not load the usual cause is a tree built on the wrong platform

docs.title: Postconditions
docs.text:
Assert Guards against dist/server.js is on the guest a transfer that stopped half way better-sqlite3 loads and takes a write a native module built for the wrong platform omniroute doctor is healthy the application's own opinion of itself storage.sqlite exists and is not empty a running server with nothing to log in to the listener is on the address the role configured the process listening somewhere else /healthz answers 200 a service that binds a port and does not serve the running process is not older than the shipped bundle a tree shipped while the service kept running /login renders a page a server that is up, healthy, and renders only 500 /v1/chat/completions answers 401 without a key an inference plane any device on the network can spend /v1 answers 401 for a bad key, and names the gate a proxy answering 401 instead of the application /api/providers answers 401 a dashboard serving an anonymous caller the unit is enabled a service that does not come back after a reboot

The key gate checks are the ones worth reading. A server that serves /v1 without a key spends the operator's provider credentials for anyone who can reach the port, and nothing else in the play would notice.

The render check is the second one worth reading. OmniRoute loads its bundle once, at start-up, so a tree that arrives while the service keeps running leaves the process serving the previous build while the new chunks sit on disk. The result is a server that is active, bound, and answering /healthz with 200, and a dashboard that answers 500 with Could not find the module "..." in the React Client Manifest. The role restarts the unit when the shipped bundle is newer than the running process, and fails the play if the disagreement survives the restart.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
The guest takes a DHCP lease, so its address moves. appctl install prints it.

# The build host. A guest, provisioned like any other application.
appctl install builder

# Build it for the guest's platform, on that host. This is the slow part —
# about 28 minutes for a 2 GB JavaScript tree.
apps/omniroute/build/omr-build-linux.sh \
  /Users/bruj0/Projects/Omniroute main

# Deploy it.
appctl install omniroute

# Second run must be changed=0.
appctl install omniroute

The checkout path above is the one this was developed against. Point the role at yours in inventory/group_vars/omrsrc/main.yml:

om_local_source: /path/to/OmniRoute

The role ships a tree; it does not fetch one. A missing checkout is refused with a message saying so, not with a failed transfer.

Then:

curl -s http://<guest>:20128/healthz        # -> ok

ok means ready. A 503 means the server is still starting; anything else means read journalctl -u omniroute -n 50 on the guest.

docs.title: The secrets
docs.text:
Five credentials, all required, none of them ever in argv:

appctl secrets set omniroute_jwt_secret            --generate
appctl secrets set omniroute_api_key_secret        --generate
appctl secrets set omniroute_storage_encryption_key --generate
appctl secrets set omniroute_initial_password       --generate
appctl secrets set omniroute_ws_bridge_secret      --generate

omniroute_initial_password is the dashboard password, applied once by the role's bootstrap step. It is not a secret the operator reads; it is a secret the application is given.

docs.title: Gotchas this role carries
docs.text:
• STORAGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY and storage.sqlite are one backup set. A rotated key leaves every stored credential undecryptable.
  • JWT_SECRET is persisted by the application when it is absent, so it is set explicitly. Otherwise a wiped state directory silently rotates it and signs every operator out.
  • The password is applied once. The role writes a stamp after the bootstrap step succeeds; without it the role would re-apply it on every play and lock the operator out.
  • om_cli is a wrapper, not a symlink. The package's own bin entry runs #!/usr/bin/env node, and nothing under app_home is on PATH on a stock guest, so it dies before the application starts.
  • A newline in a credential truncates it. systemd parses the EnvironmentFile line by line, so a value carrying one becomes a different credential rather than an error. The role asserts none of them has one.
  • The guest needs 40 GB. The tree is 2 GB and the install unpacks it.

docs.title: Add an application to DeployFlow
docs.text: An application is one directory under apps/. Nothing in common/ and nothing in playbooks/site.yml changes when you add one. If your change touches either, stop — you are about to put application knowledge in the framework, which is the one thing this layout exists to prevent.

docs.title: The two roots
docs.text:
Root Knows about Contains common/ guests, never applications lxc/ (create), python/ (contract) apps/ its own application, never guests example-app/, and whatever you add

roles_path = common:apps in ansible.cfg. An application may not require anything from another application.

docs.title: The contract: one variable
docs.text:
common/python/defaults/main.yml derives everything from app_name: app_user, app_home, app_dir, app_venv, app_state_dir, app_service_name. You set app_name and every path follows.

Two values have no derivation and you must set them: app_port and anything else unique to your app.

docs.title: 1. Scaffold
docs.text: mkdir -p apps/<name>/{defaults,tasks,meta,files}

docs.title: 2. defaults/main.yml — the whole interface
docs.text:
---
app_name: myapp          # the ONLY required value
app_port: 9000           # no derivation exists for this
app_service_name: myapp  # defaults to app_name; set only if they differ

docs.title: 3. meta/main.yml — declare the dependency, not the playbook
docs.text:
---
dependencies:
  - role: python

Ansible runs a role's dependencies before its own tasks, so common/python prepares the guest first. This is what lets a new app avoid editing any playbook. Verified: including an application runs all nine common/python tasks with python named nowhere in the playbook.

docs.title: 4. Build artifacts
docs.text:
Only for kind: repo. For kind: package the wheel already exists on PyPI and appctl build myapp says so and exits non-zero rather than failing silently.

appctl build myapp                # wheel + pinned lockfile + BUILDINFO
appctl build myapp --check        # verify committed artifacts, build nothing

defaults.python_version in app.yaml must match the interpreter the lockfile was compiled for. appctl build refuses any lock entry without a sha256, which is the same condition --require-hashes enforces at install time — caught at build time it names the package; caught at install time pip names nothing.

What is committed: the lockfile only. The wheel and BUILDINFO are gitignored, because the wheel changes on every commit and BUILDINFO records the sha256 the role checks before installing anything.

docs.title: 5. Configuration
docs.text:
If the application has settings, write them as YAML. No code.

# app.yaml
config:
  target: "{{ app_state_dir }}/config.json"
  files: [apps/myapp/config.yml]
  vars: { port: 9000 }

# apps/myapp/config.yml
server: { port: "{{ port }}", token: "${MYAPP_TOKEN}" }

appctl render turns that into JSON under tmp/rendered/<app>/, and common/python copies it to target. Set app_config_target in the role's defaults/main.yml so the framework knows where to put it.

Expect the file to be partial. Applications merge their own defaults into whatever they are given — many applications do it themselves — so only what differs from a default belongs in the YAML.

Never write a script that runs on the guest to produce configuration. That was tried here: a script merged settings into config.json on every play. The application already does that merge itself, so the script was a second implementation of the application's behaviour, shipped to every guest, free to drift from it. A two-key config.json boots the service.

Use {{ name }} for values appctl substitutes on the controller, and ${NAME} for secrets the application resolves at runtime from its EnvironmentFile. The second form is what keeps a secret out of the repository, the rendered file and the logs.

docs.title: 6. tasks/main.yml
docs.text:
Copy the closest existing role. apps/example-app/ is the reference: a wheel install, a systemd unit, a config merge, secrets, and the postconditions that prove the service answers.

Keep every postcondition — see below. They are the point of the role, not boilerplate.

Two mistakes that cost a run each, and that the reference role now avoids:

pip runs on the guest, so the lockfile must be copied there first. Pointing pip at {{ role_path }}/files/requirements.lock — a path on the controller — fails with "Could not open requirements file". That message names a missing file rather than a file that is present, on a different machine, and it looks like a broken lockfile rather than a path problem. Copy the file to {{ app_dir }}/requirements.lock and point pip at that.

The import check needs a module name, not the application name. An application name may contain a hyphen, and import example-app is a syntax error, not a missing module — so the check fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the install, and the real problem is never reached. Name the module separately (app_module), and point the unit's PYTHONPATH at the install root where it lives.

End the role by reporting what it proved. A debug task named Report the checks that passed, whose msg is a list of one line per check, becomes the check: lines in the operator's summary. Without it the summary reports a task count, which is not evidence:

- name: Report the checks that passed
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg:
      - "{{ app_name }} is installed and answering on port {{ app_port }}"
      - "import {{ app_module }}: ok"
      - "endpoint /: HTTP {{ app_endpoint.status }}"

docs.title: 7. Name the target
docs.text:
Every application says where it runs:

# app.yaml
applications:
  myapp:
    target:
      kind: proxmox_lxc      # the only implemented target
      options:
        hostname: myapp
        vmid: 121
        bind_host: 127.0.0.1  # 0.0.0.0 exposes the service to the network

kind must be a registered target. vm and docker_vm are planned and fail before anything is built, so an application that names one cannot be deployed yet. Run appctl targets to see the current list.

The manifest's pin and the role's pin must agree. source.package in app.yaml is what the operator reviews; the role pins the same thing in its own defaults/main.yml, because a role has to be able to say what it installs without reading the manifest. Those are two files, and they drift.

appctl passes the manifest's pin into the play as appctl_source_package and appctl_source_version. A role should refuse to run when they disagree:

- name: Refuse to install a package the manifest does not name
  ansible.builtin.assert:
    that:
      - appctl_source_package == app_package_name
      - appctl_source_version == app_package_version
    fail_msg: >-
      The manifest pins {{ appctl_source_package }}=={{ appctl_source_version }},
      but this role installs {{ app_package_name }}=={{ app_package_version }}.
    quiet: true

The application's name is not its package name. example-app is what the guest calls the service; bottle is what gets installed to serve it. Keep the two in separate variables, or the comparison above compares a name with itself.

options belongs to the target. The shared schema does not read inside it, so a misspelled key there is caught by the target, not by the schema.

docs.title: 8. Wire it up and deploy
docs.text:
Configuring the application in app.yaml does not deploy it. It is deployed when its name is in some guest's app_roles — that is what appctl list shows in its DEPLOYED column.

Add <name> to the guest's app_roles:

# inventory/group_vars/<group>/main.yml
app_roles:
  - myapp

The guest itself is one block in inventory/hosts.yml under lxc, plus a group that holds it. Name the group without hyphens, and do not let a group and a host share a name — Ansible rejects both with a warning that is easy to miss among a long inventory. ex and example-app is the pair to copy.

The guest block carries ansible_user, lxc_vmid and lxc_hostname. Leave the address out: Proxmox leases one and common/lxc reads it back.

docs.title: If inventory/ does not exist yet
docs.text:
inventory/ is gitignored. It names the operator's own Proxmox host, the guest IDs and the addresses of machines only they can reach — no credential in it, but not public either. A fresh clone has no inventory, and that is the expected state, not a broken checkout.

The committed templates are in inventory.example/. Create the real inventory from them:

mkdir -p inventory/group_vars
cp inventory.example/hosts.yml inventory/hosts.yml
cp -r inventory.example/group_vars/. inventory/group_vars/

Then edit the two files the quickstart names:

File What to change inventory/hosts.yml ansible_host and ansible_port for the proxmox group; the guest blocks under lxc inventory/group_vars/all/main.yml lxc_ssh_public_key — the operator's own public SSH key

The template's hosts.yml already carries one example guest and one example group, so the shape is visible before anything is edited.

Do not commit inventory/. It is in .gitignore; git add inventory/ would need -f, and the reason it is ignored is that it is the operator's own topology. If a file from it ever does land in a commit, treat it as a leak: the host names and guest IDs are not secret, but they are not public either.

docs.title: The shape of inventory/hosts.yml
docs.text:
all:
  children:
    proxmox:
      hosts:
        pve:                    # the Proxmox node itself
          ansible_host: ...
          ansible_port: 6022
          ansible_user: root
    lxc:
      hosts:
        <guest>:                # each guest the repository provisions
          ansible_user: root
          lxc_vmid: 121
          lxc_hostname: <guest>
    <group>:                   # a group per guest, holding its app_roles
      hosts:
        <guest>:

Two rules that cost an afternoon to learn:

  • The group name and the host name must differ. Ansible rejects a group that shares its name with a host, and the warning is easy to miss in a long inventory. ex / example-app is the pair to copy; mygrp / my-app is the other.
  • The group name carries no hyphen. Ansible rejects a hyphen in a group name outright.

appctl reads app_roles out of inventory/group_vars/ with a shallow scan, so the group does not have to be listed in all.children for appctl list to report the application as deployed — but Ansible needs it there for the play to reach the host, so put it in both.

docs.title: 9. Secrets
docs.text:
Declare the names in app.yaml under the application, then:

appctl secrets init                    # writes .env (0600) and .env.example
appctl secrets set myapp_api_key '...'  # or: appctl secrets set NAME --generate
appctl secrets check                   # exit 1 while any is unset

appctl install refuses to start while a required secret is absent, and names the missing keys. Never put a secret in app.yaml, in group_vars, or in a role default.

docs.title: 10. Prove it
docs.text:
appctl install myapp     # first run: expect several changed
appctl install myapp     # second run: MUST be changed=0

appctl list                     # DEPLOYED must show myapp, not "no guest"

The second run reaching changed=0 is the acceptance test. A role that reports changed every run reinstalls the tree each time and tells you nothing about its own state. See "Sentinels" below — a broken sentinel is the most common reason this test fails.

Then inject drift and confirm one re-run repairs it:

rm -f /opt/myapp/app/venv/bin/myapp     # deleted entrypoint
systemctl stop myapp && systemctl disable myapp
rm -rf /opt/myapp/state                  # mutable state must survive
appctl install myapp

For a shipped-tree application the entrypoint lives in the tree instead of the venv — delete a file the controller still has and check that rsync puts it back. Then run the play once more and require changed=0 again: drift repair that leaves the next run reporting changes has fixed the symptom and not the sentinel.

docs.title: An application that is not a Python wheel
docs.text:
Every step above assumes a wheel. An application that ships a JavaScript tree — or any prebuilt artifact with no pyproject.toml — needs the role to do the installing. apps/deepseek-harness/ is the worked example, and it is the second kind of application this repository has.

appctl build will fail on it and that is expected. build exports a git tree, optionally builds a webui bundle, then runs uv build --wheel. There is no path to "copy this tree". The app.yaml entry still needs a build block, because the schema requires one for kind: repo and appctl list prints it as the SOURCE column — say in a comment that it is inert, so the next reader does not go looking for a wheel. appctl install reads none of it: install runs the play and nothing else.

The build stays an operator act on the controller. pnpm install and pnpm run build are run by a person, not by the role, because a role that rebuilds on every play cannot tell "no changes" from "rebuilt". The role's job is to refuse to ship a tree whose install or build is older than its sources:

- name: Read the newest source file in the checkout
  # git ls-files, not a find: lib/, dist/ and node_modules are gitignored, so
  # this is exactly the set that can invalidate the build, with no build output
  # counted as an edit.
  ansible.builtin.shell:
    cmd: git -C {{ dsh_local_source | quote }} ls-files -z | xargs -0 -r stat -c %Y -- | sort -n | tail -1
  delegate_to: localhost
  become: false

Fail with the exact command to run. Comparing ages is all that is available — there is no build receipt to check against — so use stat's mtime, not mtime_epoch (see Gotchas).

Shipping the tree is one ansible.posix.synchronize from the controller:

rsync_opts: >-
  --links --times --owner --group --chown={{ app_user }}:{{ app_user }}
  --exclude=.git --exclude=**/tests
delegate_to: localhost

Each flag is load-bearing and each failure is silent — see Gotchas for what happens without them. Exclude tests and fixtures wholesale: they are the largest block of source and nothing at run time resolves through them. Use delete: true so the guest cannot keep a file the controller dropped.

The runtime goes beside the tree, not inside it. app_dir is the install root and common/python's venv already lives in it; put the shipped tree under it (app_dir/src) so the two never collide. app_state_dir stays where the framework put it, and nothing in the shipped tree is written at run time.

A runtime the template does not ship goes in as a pinned, checksummed release that the role verifies and unpacks — get_url with checksum: "sha256:…", then unarchive. Both halves of that have a gotcha below. Read the installed version back and assert it, rather than trusting a stamp file beside it.

Guest shape cannot be set per application. app.yaml's guest: block accepts only hostname, vmid, ip_optional and bind_host; anything else is rejected as an unknown key. Cores, memory and rootfs come from app.yaml defaults or from the guest's own group_vars, which is the only per-guest override.

Never run two installs against one guest. They share apt and dpkg, and the second fails on Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend, which names nothing about what actually collided.

docs.title: An application built from a source checkout
docs.text:
The second kind of shipped tree is one the controller builds rather than installs: a fork, a development branch, or any tree with no published artifact. apps/omniroute/ is the worked example — OmniRoute from main, built on a build host and served from a guest.

This is the shape the rest of this section assumes, with three differences.

The version is a commit, not a tag. A published release pins omniroute@3.8.51; a source build pins the sha the controller built from. Never pin a branch name: main moves, and a play that builds main twice reports two different artifacts. Read the sha out of the checkout and write it into the build receipt, so the guest can be asked what it is actually running.

The build must produce something the guest can run, and the role must prove it. A source tree usually has a dist/ that is gitignored, so a checkout alone is not deployable — the build is part of the artifact. The receipt therefore records the sha and the artifact it produced, and the role refuses to ship a tree whose receipt is missing, stale, or does not match the sha it was asked for.

The dependency tree is part of the artifact, not of the install. A published npm release brings its own dependencies. A source build has to npm ci before it can run at all, and the node_modules that results is what gets shipped. That tree is large, symlink-based, and must be transferred with the flags ansible.posix.synchronize needs (--links, --times) or it arrives broken or is re-transferred forever.

The role's job is to refuse, not to build. Rebuilding on every play cannot tell "no changes" from "rebuilt", so the build is an operator act on the controller and the role's job is to refuse to ship a tree that is older than its sources. Fail with the exact command to run.

The receipt is what makes the second run reach changed=0. Without it the role has nothing to compare and either reinstalls every time or trusts a mtime.

- name: Read the build receipt
  ansible.builtin.stat:
    path: "{{ om_build_receipt }}"
  delegate_to: localhost
  become: false
  register: om_receipt_stat

- name: Refuse to ship a tree that was not built from the requested commit
  ansible.builtin.fail:
    msg: >-
      {{ om_build_receipt }} is missing or does not name
      {{ om_source_ref }}. Build it on the controller:
      cd {{ om_local_source }} && git checkout {{ om_source_ref }} &&
      npm ci && npm run build:release
  when: >-
    not om_receipt_stat.stat.exists or
    (om_receipt_stat.stat.content | from_json).commit != om_source_sha

docs.title: An application whose purpose is to build another application
docs.text:
The third kind of application is a toolchain: a guest that installs no service, publishes no port, and exists so other applications can be compiled on it. apps/builder/ is the worked example.

It is worth writing because the alternative is to describe that guest as one of the two kinds that exist for shipped applications, and both are lies. A package source claims something comes from a registry — nothing does. A repo source claims there is a checkout to build — there is not one, and the schema demands a build: block that would do nothing.

So there is a third source kind, and it says exactly what it is:

builder:
  description: the guest other applications are built on
  target:
    kind: proxmox_lxc
    options:
      hostname: builder
      vmid: 123
      bind_host: 127.0.0.1
  source:
    kind: toolchain
  secrets: []

The role must not depend on common/python. That dependency is what asserts app_port is defined, and a toolchain serves nothing. A role with no dependency still runs — play 2 loops over each host's app_roles and include_roles it — so no playbook changes. Write dependencies: [] and say why in a comment, because an empty list in a role that otherwise has one looks like an oversight.

The postconditions are the whole role. A toolchain's product is a machine that can build something, so every assertion is about the machine rather than about an install:
