Assertion What it catches uname -m is x86_64 a builder running under emulation, where esbuild's Go runtime faults the runtime reports the pinned version a runtime the tree was not built against ≥ 24 GB of RAM a guest that thrashes during the build ≥ 40 GB free on the workspace a build that fails on "No space left on device" the package registry is reachable a build that fails at npm ci

Assert the minimums, not the current values. A toolchain that is too small does not fail at install — it fails hours later, during a build, with an error that names a memory limit rather than the guest. Measured: a 12 GB builder ran a build to 11.5 GB RSS, stopped answering SSH entirely, and left pct exec failing with "Cannot allocate memory - Failed to clone attached process". The play that launched it was green.

Publish the address; do not name the guest. Guest hostnames do not resolve from the controller — Proxmox's resolver is not the controller's — so a script that needs to reach the guest has to read the lease from somewhere. The lxc role already discovers it with pct exec <vmid> -- hostname -I; the toolchain role writes it to a file under tmp/, which is gitignored because the address is a DHCP lease and changes when the guest is rebuilt.

tmp/builders/builder.endpoint

host=10.0.0.80
user=root
node_dir=/opt/builder/node
work=/var/lib/builder/work

Put the user in the file, not in the script. A build script that reads host and leaves the user out gets $USER from ssh, which is not root on the controller, and the connection fails with "Too many authentication failures" — an error that looks like a credential problem and is not one.

A toolchain's runtime is pinned in one place. If the build script also installs the runtime, there are two copies of the version and they drift. The role installs it, checksummed, and the build script asserts it is there and fails with a named error. That is the difference between an environment that is provisioned and one that is whatever apt-get returned that day.

docs.title: Postconditions: non-negotiable
docs.text:
Every role must assert the result, not the exit code. These four caught real bugs that a green play hid:

Assert Guards against the CLI runs (myapp --version) a deleted entrypoint with the package intact the package imports (python -c "import myapp") a half-installed tree that still has a console script the app's own data exists (a row, a file) a running server with nothing to log in to ss -ltn shows the requested address the process listening somewhere you did not ask for

Assert the authority the process reports, not the one you asked for. The strongest form of the last row: read the listener's own URL from its log, and fail unless it carries the address the role configured. Rebuilding the URL from a variable asserts what the role already believes and proves nothing about what is running. Do that read inside the guest, in one shell step, when the value is a credential — the launch token of an authenticated service is a live credential for the life of the process, and a task that interpolates it puts it in the controller's log.

Wait for the service before asserting on it. systemd returns from start when it accepts the job, which is seconds before a composed application binds. wait_for on the port, and on the state file, so the assertions that follow read a running service. An empty ss reading during boot is indistinguishable from address drift, and a drift check that cannot tell the difference restarts a service that was starting correctly.

Do not use --force on an app's init command. A failed init leaves a half-written state directory and refuses to run again; --force destroys the database on top of that. Recovery means deleting the state directory.

Pass secrets through the environment, never argv. ps is world-readable on the guest.

docs.title: Sentinels: the four ways to break changed=0
docs.text:
Every one of these shipped green. All were found by running the play twice and asking why the second run still reported changes. Read this section before writing the checks in tasks/main.yml.

A sentinel that can never succeed is worse than no sentinel. It looks like a guard, it passes review, and it silently keeps a gate permanently open so the role reinstalls itself forever.

Trap Why it is always wrong 'changed' in stdout matches "unchanged". Use == 'changed' after a trim. an import of a name that does not exist the class may live in a different module. Verify the import on the guest before trusting it. a glob consumed by next() twice next(g, None) and (next(g) / 'f') takes the only match on the first call and raises StopIteration on the second. Materialise with list(). a changed_when test that is true when nothing changed always compare the whole value, not a substring

docs.title: Greedy regexes and block scalars
docs.text:
Both of these cost real time and neither raises an error.

# WRONG: greedy, matches up to the LAST colon, so '127.0.0.1:18790' -> '18790'
| map('regex_replace', '^.*:', '')

# WRONG: a YAML block scalar is literal, so Jinja reads \d as an escaped
# backslash and the regex matches a literal backslash. Strips nothing.
| map('regex_replace', ':\\d+$', '')

# RIGHT: strip by the numeric port, then trim
| map('trim')
| map('regex_replace', ':\d+$', '')

A trailing newline survives unless you trim, and a trimmed value still fails to equal an untrimmed expectation. Check both sides.

docs.title: Gotchas, all measured on this host
docs.text:
• The framework must have no default for app_name or app_port. A role's meta dependency has its defaults applied after the including role's own, so a default in common/python silently overrides the application's and the guest gets the wrong paths. It stayed hidden while there was one application, because its name happened to equal the default. Do not add one back.
  • .j2 files belong in templates/, not files/. ansible.builtin.template resolves src from templates/; in files/ it fails with "Could not find or access". The .j2 suffix is the tell.
  • playbook_dir is playbooks/, not the repo root. Use lxc_repo_root from group_vars/all for controller paths. A role default will not do: it does not exist on localhost, which is where delegate_to: localhost puts the lookup.
  • app_name must be a valid path segment. It is interpolated into app_home, app_dir and app_venv without sanitising.
  • virtualenv_command is a command line, not a path. Use "{{ app_venv }}/bin/python -m venv". Hardcoding /usr/bin/python3 lets the interpreter and the venv drift apart silently.
  • The pip module takes requirements:, never name: for a lockfile path. name parses its argument as a requirement and rejects a path.
  • --no-deps is required alongside --require-hashes. With hashes present pip cannot resolve, so every package must already be named in the file.
  • Gate the install on the lockfile changing or the package being absent. The pip module reports changed every time it runs, which is what stops a settled play from reinstalling 200 wheels on each run.
  • Playwright's cache is chromium-1243, not chromium_headless_shell-*. A sentinel using the headless-shell name never matches and re-downloads 115 MB every run. Assert on a versioned directory, not on the cache root.
  • playwright install-deps takes no --with-deps and reports changed on every invocation. Gate it on a library it must install, e.g. dpkg-query -W -f=${Status} libnss3.
  • Pin PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH to the account the service runs as, or the browser lands in root's cache where the service cannot see it.
  • A venv left by an older template is a trap. It installs wheels for the interpreter it was built with and fails at the first compiled import. common/python asserts the version and fails loudly; keep that check.
  • unarchive defaults to the controller, not the guest. Fetching a tarball with get_url and then unpacking it needs remote_src: true, or the module looks for the path on the controller and fails with "Could not find or access … on the Ansible Controller" while the file sits on the guest. remote_src then makes it refuse a dest that does not exist, so create the directory first — the two errors name the wrong thing.
  • synchronize skips symlinks and resets mtimes. Both are fatal for a JavaScript tree and neither is reported. Without --links, a pnpm node_modules arrives with its packages but an empty node_modules/@deepseek-ai/, and every entry point fails ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND for a package that is present. Without --times, synchronize's own --delay-updates stages each file under a temporary name and renames it at the end of the run, which gives every file a fresh mtime — so the next run's quick check sees the whole tree as different and transfers all of it again, reporting changed forever. The play never settles.
  • stat has no mtime_epoch on ansible-core 2.16. It returns float seconds in mtime. Asking for the removed key fails the conditional with "'dict object' has no attribute 'mtime_epoch'", which reads like a missing file rather than a missing field.
  • The stock Ubuntu template ships no curl. A shell assertion that probes the service with it retries to its timeout against "command not found" and reports a broken service that is serving perfectly well. Install it in the role, or use ansible.builtin.uri.
  • A runtime installed under a version directory is not on PATH, and its own bin shims then fail. Every bin/* entry of such a runtime is #!/usr/bin/env node, so running {{ dsh_node_dir }}/bin/corepack dies with env: 'node': No such file or directory before the tool starts. Invoke the interpreter by absolute path on the tool's JS entry instead. The same applies to any package.json bin a guest should expose: a symlink to it runs whatever node PATH finds, which on a stock guest is nothing at all — write a wrapper that names the pinned interpreter, DSH_HOME and the state the tool expects.
  • Read a version from the artifact that was built, not from a second copy of it. A package manager version belongs in the project's own packageManager field; a guest that hard-codes it can end up holding a tool the tree was never built with, and the mismatch surfaces at use, not at install.
  • A host with no fixed address cannot be asserted by name. Assert the address the process reports it bound, not a configured one, or the assertion tests the inventory rather than the service.
  • df --output=avail -B M prints a unit suffix, and | int on 55579M is 0. A disk assertion that reads 0 MB free fails for the wrong reason, and the message says "too small" when the disk is full of room. Use -B1 and divide, or strip the suffix.
  • df --output prints a header row above the value. The value is the last line of stdout, not the whole of it.
  • The command module never runs a shell. df … | tail -1 arrives as two arguments named | and tail and fails with a non-zero exit. Pipe in Jinja, or make the command print one value and nothing else.
  • A regex inside a YAML string inside a Jinja expression needs four layers of escaping, and it fails as NoneType has no attribute group rather than as a syntax error. When a value has to be parsed, make the command print a bare number: awk '/^MemTotal:/ {print $2}' /proc/meminfo beats a regex_search on grep MemTotal /proc/meminfo.
  • get_url is only idempotent if the file stays. A task that downloads a tarball, unpacks it and then deletes the tarball re-downloads 31 MB on every run and reports changed forever. Keep the download in a cache directory.
  • A set_fact whose value is a plain integer string fails the play with "Conditional result (True) was derived from value of type 'str'". Pipe it through | bool or compare against a typed value.

docs.title: Adding a guest, not an app
docs.text:
Different task. One block in inventory/hosts.yml, no address — Proxmox leases one and common/lxc reads it back:

lxc:
  hosts:
    my-app:
      ansible_user: root
      lxc_vmid: 121
      lxc_hostname: my-app

Plus a group that holds it, and a group_vars/<group>/main.yml that says what the guest runs. Remember the group name and the host name must differ, and the group name carries no hyphen.

inventory/ is gitignored — it holds the operator's own topology, not the project's. If it does not exist, create it from inventory.example/ first:

mkdir -p inventory/group_vars
cp inventory.example/hosts.yml inventory/hosts.yml
cp -r inventory.example/group_vars/. inventory/group_vars/

Do not commit it. See "If inventory/ does not exist yet" above for the full procedure.

Read docs/PLAN-proxmox-lxc-ansible.md before changing anything in common/. Section 8 is a list of failures that passed review and only showed up under test; several of them produce a green play and a broken service.

docs.title: AGENTS.md
docs.text: How to work in this repository. Read this before changing anything.

docs.title: What this is
docs.text:
Application delivery to a deployment target. A stock Ubuntu template goes in, Ansible configures it, the application runs under systemd with a sha256-pinned dependency tree. No container image is ever built.

appctl is the tool: it builds artifacts, delivers them through the named target, and manages secrets. It is the intended entry point for everything.

docs.title: The two boundaries that matter
docs.text:
app.yaml        configuration: applications, targets, builds, secrets
common/         framework. Names no application, anywhere.
  lxc/          pct create from a stock template, DHCP, address discovery
  python/       toolchain, service account, venv — the contract
apps/           one directory per application
  example-app/  the sample used by the quickstart
  builder/      a toolchain: a guest that exists to build other applications
src/appctl/     the appctl package
  targets/      where an application runs; proxmox_lxc is the only one built
inventory/      the operator's own guests. GITIGNORED, and absent on a fresh
                clone; inventory.example/ holds the templates.

roles_path = common:apps. A role's meta dependency declares what it needs, so a new application never edits a playbook.

An application must not require anything from another application, and common/ and src/appctl/ must never name one. If your change makes the framework aware of a specific app, it is in the wrong place — put it in apps/<name>/.

The shared code must not name a target. pct, the container ID, the template, the storage, the bridge and the guest network live in src/appctl/targets/proxmox_lxc.py. A module outside targets/ that mentions one of them is in the wrong place. A new target is a new file under targets/, and it does not change config.py.

A role that installs no service does not depend on common/python. That dependency is what asserts app_port is defined, and a toolchain serves nothing. A role with no dependency still runs — play 2 loops over each host's app_roles and include_roles it — so no playbook changes. See apps/builder/meta/main.yml.

A toolchain's product is a machine that can build, so its role asserts the machine. Not the exit code of the install commands. A guest that is too small does not fail at install — it fails hours later, during a build, with an error that names a memory limit rather than the guest.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
uv tool install --editable .       # or: uv pip install -e .

appctl list                        # every app, its target, and last install
appctl targets                     # implemented targets, and the planned ones
appctl secrets check               # required secrets present? exit 1 if not
appctl render                      # YAML -> JSON, without deploying
appctl build example-app           # wheel + pinned lockfile + BUILDINFO
appctl install example-app         # deliver one application; the name is positional
appctl install                     # valid only when exactly one is configured

The application name is a positional argument, not a flag. Flags follow it, and anything after a bare -- is passed to ansible-playbook untouched:

appctl install example-app -q                # terse
appctl install example-app --forks 4         # guests at once
appctl install example-app -- --check --diff # straight to ansible-playbook

Use the -- form for anything the tool also defines. Passing --quiet without it does nothing useful, because ansible-playbook has no such option.

Run logs are kept and never pruned. Each run writes commands.txt, log.txt, recap.txt, errors.txt and meta.txt under tmp/runs/TIMESTAMP/. Read commands.txt first; log.txt is mostly SSH plumbing.

docs/architecture.md lists the invariants. Read it before changing a role: several of them are failures that passed review and only showed up under test, and several produce a green play and a broken service.

docs.title: The tool
docs.text:
The tool is appctl in src/appctl/. Its own documentation is in docs/, and it takes precedence over this file for anything about the tool:

docs/README.md the index docs/architecture.md how it fits together, and where the target boundary is docs/configuration.md every key in app.yaml docs/build-pipeline.md the two build paths docs/rendering.md how YAML becomes the configuration the guest reads docs/secrets.md how a secret reaches the guest docs/targets.md the target interface, and how to add a target docs/site.md the documentation site: how it is assembled and how to publish it

docs.title: Adding an application
docs.text:
Read .agents/skills/deployflow-add-app/SKILL.md first. It has the full process, the postconditions a role must carry, and the sentinel traps.

The short version: one directory under apps/, an entry in app.yaml, and changed=0 on the second appctl install. Nothing in common/ or playbooks/ changes.

docs.title: Rules that are not stylistic
docs.text:
A provider may need no secret at all. Some model providers authenticate with OAuth: the guest holds a token in its own state directory, and nothing secret belongs in this repository for them. An assertion that demands an API key for an OAuth provider is a wrong requirement, not a safe one — it blocks a run that is correct. Read the application's defaults/main.yml before changing that.

Secrets. .env at the repo root, gitignored, mode 0600, written by appctl secrets set. NAME value and NAME --generate are both supported; the bare form prompts. .env.example is committed and lists which keys are required. Never put a secret in app.yaml, in group_vars, or in a role default. Never pass one in argv — it is visible in ps. appctl redacts password-shaped values from the logs it writes.

ansible-vault is gone. The vault file this repo used was encrypted with a throwaway password that was then deleted, which made it undecryptable and unrecoverable. Do not reintroduce it.

Guests get a DHCP lease, not an address. Proxmox's SDN zone hands one out and registers the hostname; common/lxc reads it back with pct exec <vmid> -- hostname -I and sets ansible_host. A statically addressed Ubuntu 26.04 guest comes up with no IPv4 at all and systemd-networkd exiting 243/CREDENTIALS. Do not add an address to the inventory.

appctl install refuses to guess. With several applications deployed it stops and prints the exact command to run. Configuring an application does not deploy it — only an app_roles entry does, and appctl list shows which is which. Secrets are checked for the selected application only; requiring them all up front lets one you are not deploying block one you are.

appctl install X also runs the lxc tag. Play 1 is what discovers the lease; without it play 2 cannot resolve the guest. It is guarded by a stat, so on an existing guest it costs a few no-op tasks.

Configure with YAML, not with code. An application's settings live in apps/<name>/config.yml and are rendered on the controller by appctl render, which install runs for you. common/python copies the result to app_config_target. Do not add a script to files/ that runs on the guest to produce configuration: the application merges its own defaults into whatever it is given, so a second implementation is redundant and free to drift. Use {{ name }} for controller substitution and ${NAME} for runtime secrets; the second form is what keeps a secret out of the repository.

Never round-trip app.yaml through a YAML dumper. It carries a comment above nearly every setting, explaining why it is what it is, and yaml.safe_dump destroys all of them — measured, 18 comment lines in and 0 out. Anything that writes configuration must edit the slice it owns and leave the rest byte-identical. That is what src/appctl/state.py does: it rewrites only the state: block, and refuses rather than guesses when it cannot find it.

state: is tool-written. A build or an install fills it in. Do not hand-edit it, and do not add sections to it: only built and installed are accepted, and anything else would be silently dropped by the next write. It lives in a committed file, so every run is a diff — that is the trade for having the record next to the thing it describes.

Unknown config keys are an error. app.yaml is strictly validated on purpose: a misspelled key would otherwise be dropped and the service would come up on the wrong port.

docs.title: Sentinels: the trap that wastes the most time
docs.text:
Every task that checks a precondition is a sentinel, and a sentinel that can never succeed is worse than none — it looks like a guard and silently keeps a gate permanently open, so the role reinstalls itself on every play.

All of these shipped green here and were found only by running the play twice:

Trap Fix 'changed' in stdout matches "unchanged". Use == 'changed' after trim importing a name that does not exist check the import on the guest before trusting it a glob read by next() twice StopIteration. Materialise with list() regex_replace '^.*:' greedy: keeps the port, not the host ':\\d+$' in a YAML block scalar block scalars are literal; Jinja reads \\d as an escaped backslash and matches nothing

The acceptance test for any role change is changed=0 on a second appctl install. If it reports changes, one of the above is the reason.

docs.title: Verified state
docs.text:
Measured on Proxmox VE 9.2.3:

  • Base Ubuntu 26.04, Python 3.14.4
  • appctl install <app> → a settled run reports changed=0
  • appctl build <app> → byte-identical wheel for the same commit

These are observations from one node, not a benchmark. Do not quote them as a comparison with another deployment system.

Drift repair in one re-run: deleted entrypoint, stopped and disabled unit, deleted state directory. A first settle after a real change takes longer, because the built tree crosses the link.

docs.title: Before you commit
docs.text:
• ansible-playbook --syntax-check playbooks/site.yml
  • appctl secrets check — a run needs these
  • git status must not show .env, tmp/, apps/*/files/dist/, tools/, or inventory/
  • appctl install <app> twice: the second must be changed=0
  • git diff app.yaml shows only the state: block changed, never the comments
  • pytest tests passes
  • python scripts/build_site_docs.py --clean && mkdocs build --strict — if you changed a document, a link, or a diagram. python scripts/serve_docs.py does the same and watches the sources.

docs.title: The inventory is not in git
docs.text:
inventory/ is gitignored. It names the operator's own Proxmox host, the guest IDs and the addresses of machines only they can reach.

Nothing in it is a credential, and none of it is public either — which is exactly why it does not belong in a repository that a stranger can clone. The committed templates are in inventory.example/, and a fresh clone creates the real inventory from them:

mkdir -p inventory/group_vars
cp inventory.example/hosts.yml inventory/hosts.yml
cp -r inventory.example/group_vars/. inventory/group_vars/

Two things follow from the directory being absent on a fresh clone, and both are expected rather than broken:

  • appctl list reports every application as "no guest", because it finds no app_roles. That is the truth about a clone with no inventory.
  • The CI syntax check runs against inventory.example/hosts.yml, which exercises the same playbook and the same role paths.

Do not commit inventory/. It is in .gitignore, so git add inventory/ would need -f — and if a file from it ever lands in a commit, treat it as a leak. The host names and guest IDs are not secret, but they are not public.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Read AGENTS.md first. It holds the rules that are not stylistic.

docs.title: Before you commit
docs.text:
pytest tests -q
ansible-playbook --syntax-check -i inventory/hosts.yml playbooks/site.yml
appctl install <app>   # twice; the second must report changed=0

git status must not show .env, tmp/, apps/*/files/dist/, tools/ or inventory/.

inventory/ is gitignored. It names your own Proxmox host, the guest IDs and the addresses of machines only you can reach. A fresh clone has no inventory at all, and that is the expected state — the committed templates live in inventory.example/, and the skill documents how to create the real one:

mkdir -p inventory/group_vars
cp inventory.example/hosts.yml inventory/hosts.yml
cp -r inventory.example/group_vars/. inventory/group_vars/

The syntax check above therefore needs a local inventory. On a fresh clone, use the template instead — it exercises the same playbook and role paths:

ansible-playbook --syntax-check -i inventory.example/hosts.yml playbooks/site.yml

docs.title: What a change must preserve
docs.text:
• An application is one directory. Nothing in common/ or playbooks/ changes when you add one.
  • The shared code names no application and no target. pct and the guest network live in src/appctl/targets/proxmox_lxc.py.
  • Every role checks that its application works. A green playbook is not evidence of a working service.
  • A second run reports changed=0. A role that reports a change every run is reinstalling itself and says nothing about its own state.
  • An unknown key is an error. A misspelled key would otherwise be a silent no-op.

docs.title: DeployFlow
docs.text:
Point your coding agent at this repository and tell it to install an application. It writes the deployment, you review it, and the service is verified before anyone calls it done.

The current landscape. Open the diagram.

DeployFlow is a workflow for delivering applications to servers. It defines what an application needs, how it should be installed, and how we know it actually works. The agent does the writing. The workflow does the proving.

The current implementation delivers to a container on a Proxmox host with Ansible. That is the first destination, not the definition of the project. The workflow itself — manifest, roles, checks, verification — is what transfers when the next destination arrives.

docs.title: The problem it solves
docs.text:
An agent can write a deployment in a few minutes. What it cannot do, on its own, is tell you the deployment is correct:

  • The playbook finished green. That proves Ansible ran, not that the service works. A database file exists on a server that was never bootstrapped, and a process binds the wrong port — both produce a green play.
  • The same steps run on every machine, and the differences between machines are where deployments break.
  • The knowledge of "how this application should be installed" lives in someone's head, and leaves when they do.
  • The next person, or the next agent, starts from nothing.

DeployFlow turns that into a repository an agent can work inside:

The application declares itself A manifest says where it comes from, what it needs, and what "working" means for it. The agent writes the delivery A role per application, generated against a documented contract, reviewable before it runs. The workflow proves it works Each application carries its own checks, and they run after every install. The steps are repeatable A second install on the same inputs changes nothing, and says so. The knowledge is in the repo The next agent reads it instead of guessing.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Four steps. The first two are the setup every run needs; the third is the one that proves the workflow works; the fourth is how you add your own application.

docs.title: 1. Get the tool
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/bruj0/deployflow.git
cd deployflow
uv tool install --editable .

appctl is the command this repository is built around. It needs Python 3.12 or later, and it needs ansible-playbook on your PATH:

uv tool install ansible-core     # or: pipx install ansible-core

The manifest is gitignored too — app.yaml is yours, and the committed template is app.example.yaml. Copy it:

cp app.example.yaml app.yaml

docs.title: 2. Create your inventory
docs.text:
The inventory names your Proxmox host, your guest IDs and the addresses of machines only you can reach. It is gitignored, so a fresh clone has none — and that is the expected state, not a broken checkout. The committed templates are in inventory.example/:

mkdir -p inventory/group_vars
cp inventory.example/hosts.yml inventory/hosts.yml
cp -r inventory.example/group_vars/. inventory/group_vars/

Then edit the two files the templates name:

File What to put in it inventory/hosts.yml your Proxmox host and your guests inventory/group_vars/all/main.yml your SSH public key

docs.title: 3. Install an application and watch it prove itself
docs.text:
The repository ships example-app: a small HTTP service that installs from a pinned wheel and checks that it answers. It needs no build host and no half-hour compile, so it is the fastest way to see the whole workflow.

appctl install example-app

The last lines are the point of the whole exercise:

example-app: proxmox_lxc -> example-app  10 changed, 0 failed, 41 tasks, 33s
  check: example-app is installed and answering on port 8080
  check: import example_app: ok
  check: unit example-app: active
  check: listener on 8080: present
  check: endpoint /: HTTP 200

Those five lines are the application's own checks, not a task count. Each one stands in for a failure that a green play would otherwise hide.

Now run it again:

appctl install example-app

example-app: proxmox_lxc -> example-app  0 changed, 0 failed, 41 tasks, 29s
  check: example-app is installed and answering on port 8080
  check: import example_app: ok
  check: unit example-app: active
  check: listener on 8080: present
  check: endpoint /: HTTP 200

0 changed is the claim this project makes. The second run found nothing to do and re-verified the service anyway. A tool that reports a change every run is reinstalling itself and proving nothing.

docs.title: 4. Add your own application
docs.text:
Do not write the role by hand. There is a skill for it, and your agent can follow it:

Read AGENTS.md and .agents/skills/deployflow-add-app/SKILL.md, then add support for . Use the deployflow-add-app skill. Show me the diff before you run anything.

The skill covers the manifest, the role, the pinned lockfile, the checks, and the traps that make a run reinstall itself forever. It also documents how to create the inventory above when it is missing.

To look around first:

appctl targets      # which destinations exist, and which are not built yet
appctl list         # what this repository has configured

docs.title: The other three applications
docs.text:
example-app is the smallest thing that works. Three others ship as worked examples of the shapes that are harder:

Application What it shows What it costs omniroute-release an application installed from a published release five generated secrets, no build omniroute an application built from a checkout a checkout, a build host, ~28 min builder the build host the second one needs 24 GB of RAM on the host

omniroute-release is the one to run next if you want a real service: it needs no builder and no compile.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The workflow, lane by lane. Open the diagram. 

you:  "install a new application"
agent: reads the contract, writes the manifest and the role,
       runs the checks, reports what it changed and what it verified
you:   reviews the diff, approves the run
run:   installs the pinned artifact, then checks the service actually answers

Five parts:

Where each part lives. Open the diagram.

docs.title: 1. The manifest
docs.text:
What an application is: where its code comes from, what configuration it takes, which secrets it needs, and which destination runs it. One file, app.yaml:

applications:
  myapp:
    description: what it is, in one line
    target:
      kind: proxmox_lxc        # the destination that runs it
      options:
        hostname: myapp
        vmid: 121
    source:
      kind: repo               # a checkout, built here
      repo: /path/to/myapp
      ref: HEAD
    build:
      python_version: "3.14"
      verify_lock: true        # refuse a lock entry with no hash
    config:
      target: "{{ app_state_dir }}/config.json"
      files:
        - apps/myapp/config.yml
      vars:
        app_port: 9000
    secrets:
      - myapp_api_key

The source: block says where the code comes from. There are three kinds, because there are three genuinely different things to say:

Kind What it is What has to happen first package a published version nothing — the artifact already exists repo a commit in a checkout the artifact has to be built toolchain nothing at all — the application is the environment the role assembles it

The third is the unusual one, and it is what makes the workflow general enough to build the other two. It is explained in Three kinds of application.

source.package is the pin the operator reviews, and the role checks that it installs the same thing. If the manifest says bottle==0.13.3 and the role pins a different version, the install refuses to run rather than quietly installing something else. The application's name is not its package name: example-app is what the guest calls the service, bottle is what gets installed to serve it.

docs.title: 2. The application role
docs.text:
How it is installed, in one directory per application. The agent writes this; it follows the contract in AGENTS.md:

# apps/myapp/tasks/main.yml
- name: Copy the lockfile to the guest
  # pip on the guest cannot open a path on the controller, so the file
  # travels first and pip is pointed at where it landed.
  ansible.builtin.copy:
    src: "{{ role_path }}/files/requirements.lock"
    dest: "{{ app_dir }}/requirements.lock"
    mode: "0644"

- name: Install the application
  ansible.builtin.pip:
    requirements: "{{ app_dir }}/requirements.lock"
    virtualenv: "{{ app_venv }}"
    extra_args: "--require-hashes"

- name: Check that the application answers a request
  ansible.builtin.uri:
    url: "http://127.0.0.1:{{ app_port }}/"
  register: app_endpoint
  failed_when: false

- name: Fail when the application does not answer
  ansible.builtin.fail:
    msg: "The service listens but does not answer"
  when: app_endpoint.status is undefined

- name: Report the checks that passed
  # This task is what the summary prints. Its lines become the `check:` lines
  # the operator reads, so the evidence the application gave is the evidence
  # that is reported.
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg:
      - "{{ app_name }} is installed and answering on port {{ app_port }}"
      - "endpoint /: HTTP {{ app_endpoint.status }}"

docs.title: 3. The target
docs.text:
Where it runs. The manifest names one, and the target owns everything about that destination:

# src/appctl/targets/proxmox_lxc.py
@register
class ProxmoxLxcTarget(Target):
    kind = "proxmox_lxc"
    summary = "an application installed into a Proxmox LXC guest with Ansible"

    def validate(self, context):
        """Reject a bad setup before anything is built or started."""
        if not context.app().target.options.get("hostname"):
            raise TargetError("target is missing: hostname")

    def deploy(self, context, artifacts, rendered):
        """Install it, run its checks, and report what was observed."""
        ...

Two more destinations are named so a manifest can ask for them and get a clear answer, but they are not built yet:

$ appctl targets
implemented targets:
  proxmox_lxc: an application installed into a Proxmox LXC guest with Ansible
planned, not implemented:
  docker_vm: provision a virtual machine and run the application in Docker there
  vm: provision a virtual machine and install the application into it

docs.title: 4. The checks
docs.text:
The part most tools skip. A deployment is not done when the command succeeds. It is done when the service answers. Each application carries its own checks, because only the application knows what "working" means for it:

# apps/myapp/tasks/main.yml
- name: Check that the package imports
  ansible.builtin.command:
    argv: ["{{ app_venv }}/bin/python", "-c", "import myapp"]
  changed_when: false

- name: Check that the service is listening on the requested port
  ansible.builtin.command:
    argv: [ss, -ltn]
  changed_when: false
  register: app_listeners

- name: Fail when the service is not listening on the requested port
  ansible.builtin.fail:
    msg: "The service is running but not listening on port {{ app_port }}"
  when: app_port | string not in app_listeners.stdout

The port check matters more than it looks. systemctl is-active says the process is up; it does not say the process bound the port you asked for. A service that came up on 8000 instead of 9000 passes an is-active check and fails every request.

docs.title: 5. Secrets
docs.text:
appctl secrets manages a single file: .env at the repository root, mode 0600, gitignored. It is the only plain-text copy of a secret on the controller.

appctl secrets init                       # write .env (0600) and .env.example
appctl secrets check                      # what is required and still missing
appctl secrets list                       # names and state, never values

init reads the secrets: blocks in app.yaml and creates one key per secret, empty, so a fresh clone knows exactly what to fill in. .env.example — the list of required keys with no values — is committed, so the next person sees what the deployment needs without seeing anything it should not.

Setting a value has three forms, and the first is the one to reach for:

appctl secrets set myapp_api_key                   # prompts; the value never reaches argv or shell history
appctl secrets set myapp_api_key '<value>'         # positional
appctl secrets set myapp_api_key --generate        # random value, 32 bytes of entropy

--generate takes several names at once, which is how the shipped applications are set up — all five OmniRoute credentials are issued by the system itself:

appctl secrets set omniroute_jwt_secret omniroute_api_key_secret \
                     omniroute_storage_encryption_key \
                     omniroute_initial_password omniroute_ws_bridge_secret \
                     --generate

set rewrites the file in place, preserving existing keys and their order, so running it twice for one key leaves one entry — a duplicate KEY in a .env is a well-known source of "I changed it and nothing happened".

Use --generate for a secret this system issues for itself. It is wrong for anything with an external issuer: a provider API key has to come from the provider, not from a random string.

check exits 1 while anything required is unset, which is what makes it usable in CI. appctl install runs the same check before it touches the cluster, because discovering a missing secret halfway through a play leaves half the guest configured.

Where State .env on the controller the only plain-text copy, mode 0600, gitignored the temporary extra-vars file mode 0600, passed as --extra-vars @file, deleted at exit the guest's EnvironmentFile mode 0640, owned by root:<service account> — systemd reads it as PID 1, and the service account has to be able to read it too the application's memory resolved from that file at startup any log never

A secret is never written to app.yaml, to a rendered config file, or to a log. In a config file it appears only as a ${NAME} reference, which the guest resolves at startup — that is what makes a config file safe to commit.

Full detail, including the three ways a secret leaks and the guard for each: docs/secrets.md.

docs.title: Three kinds of application
docs.text:
Most applications come from somewhere: a registry, or a checkout. Some applications are somewhere — they are the machine other applications are built on, and they install nothing at all.

That is the third kind, and the workflow needs it to describe its own build hosts honestly:

builder:
  description: the guest other applications are built on
  target:
    kind: proxmox_lxc
    options:
      hostname: builder
      vmid: 123
  source:
    kind: toolchain          # no package, no repo, no build
  secrets: []

A toolchain application:

  • installs no service and publishes no port;
  • has no artifact, so appctl build on it says so and exits non-zero rather than silently succeeding;
  • has no dependency on common/python — that dependency is what asserts app_port is defined, and a build host serves nothing;
  • asserts the machine, not the install. Its role checks that the guest is the right architecture, that the runtime is the pinned one, that it has enough memory and disk, and that it can reach the package registry. A role that installs a compiler and reports success has not said anything about whether a build can run on it.

That last point is the difference that matters, and it is measured. A builder created with 12 GB of RAM passed every install check and then failed during a build, with an error that named a memory limit and not the guest — and the guest stopped answering SSH entirely. The role now asserts the floor it needs before the build starts.

The worked example is apps/builder/.

docs.title: Ready-to-use applications
docs.text: The repository ships four applications that work, not three that illustrate. example-app is covered in Try it above; the other three cover the shapes that are harder.

docs.title: omniroute-release — an application installed from a published release
docs.text:
OmniRoute is a Next.js server with a native SQLite binding, served by one systemd unit on one guest.

This one is installed from a published npm release: the guest's own npm install fetches a pinned version, and nothing OmniRoute-related runs on the controller. It is the shape an application takes when its code already ships as an artifact.

appctl install omniroute-release
appctl install omniroute-release        # must report changed=0

See apps/omniroute-release/ for what the role asserts and why the credentials file is group-readable.

docs.title: omniroute — an application built from a source checkout
docs.text: The same application, built from the upstream main branch instead of installed from npm. It is the shape an application takes when there is no published artifact — a fork, a development branch — and the build has to happen on a guest of its own.

docs.title: builder — the build host
docs.text:
The guest the OmniRoute build runs on. It installs a compiler, a pinned Node and a workspace, and it installs no service of its own.

appctl install builder

It publishes its address to tmp/builders/builder.endpoint, because guest hostnames do not resolve from the controller — Proxmox's resolver is not the controller's — and a build script that cannot find the machine cannot use it.

See apps/builder/.

docs.title: What you get when the agent does it
docs.text:
A reviewer reading the diff sees the intent, not a wall of generated YAML:

  • the manifest block for the new application,
  • one role directory with the install steps and the checks,
  • a pinned dependency lockfile, so the tree that installs is the tree that was reviewed,
  • a recorded state: block saying what was built and when it was last installed.

The agent's own reasoning stays in its session. What lands in the repository is declarative and reviewable.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
Every feature, what it gives you, and the file that holds it.

Feature What it gives you Where Deterministic flow appctl drives the same order every run — validate, check secrets, render, then play — and exits non-zero on failure. src/appctl/cli.py Agentic skill The contract, the scaffold and the checklist, so an agent writes a role that matches the others. .agents/skills/deployflow-add-app/SKILL.md App manifest One file describes every application: source, config, secrets, destination. Unknown keys are an error, so a typo fails loudly. app.example.yaml Private inventory Your hosts, guest IDs and addresses stay out of git. The repository ships templates and the skill documents how to build the real one. inventory.example/ Pinned artifacts Every dependency pinned by hash. The build refuses a lockfile without one, and the role checks the manifest and the role agree on the version. src/appctl/build.py Application-level checks Each app checks that it imports, is active, listens where it was asked to, and answers a request. The result is printed as check: lines, so the summary is evidence rather than a task count. apps/example-app/tasks/main.yml Idempotency A second install reports changed=0, which proves the run is repeatable rather than reinstalling itself. src/appctl/install.py Secrets management appctl secrets keeps them in a gitignored .env; the run reads them from a mode-0600 file, so they never reach argv or a log. src/appctl/secrets.py Pluggable targets A target interface separates "what the application is" from "where it runs". One target ships today. src/appctl/targets/base.py Streaming logs The play streams as it runs, with a heartbeat when a task goes quiet, and keeps commands, log, recap and errors per run under tmp/runs/. src/appctl/install.py Shared framework The toolchain, the service account and the venv that every application role depends on. common/python/ Four working applications A sample that installs in one command, a service from a published release, a service built from a checkout, and the build host that builds it. apps/example-app/, apps/omniroute-release/, apps/omniroute/, apps/builder/

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The words this document uses, in the order a newcomer meets them.

Word What it means here appctl The command-line tool. It validates, renders and installs. manifest (app.yaml) One file describing every application: where it comes from, what config it takes, which secrets it needs, where it runs. Gitignored — the committed template is app.example.yaml. role A directory under apps/<name>/ holding the install steps and the checks for one application. target Where an application runs. proxmox_lxc ships; vm and docker_vm are named but not built. inventory Which machines exist. inventory/hosts.yml plus group_vars/. Gitignored, because it names your own hosts. group_vars/ Per-group settings, read by Ansible. all/ holds what every guest needs; each other directory holds one group's. guest The machine an application is installed into — here, a Proxmox LXC container. controller The machine you run appctl on. It renders and drives; it does not serve. artifact The thing that gets installed: a pinned wheel, a built tree, a published release. pin An exact version, and for a Python dependency the sha256 of the file behind it. lockfile (requirements.lock) Every dependency and its hashes, so the tree that installs is the tree that was reviewed. changed=0 The second run found nothing to do. The project's central claim. toolchain An application that installs no service: the build host other applications are built on.

docs.title: To run a delivery on the current target
docs.text:
Requirement Detail A Proxmox VE host You need pct and SSH access to it. A cached Linux template on that host The guest is created from it. SSH access from the controller to the host The framework drives pct over SSH. ansible-playbook on the controller The play does the configuring. Python 3.12 or later on the controller That is the CLI's own requirement. Nothing else for the sample example-app installs from a public wheel, so it needs no checkout, no build host and no secrets.

For the omniroute application specifically, three more things are needed, and all three are consequences of building from source rather than installing a release:

Requirement Why A checkout of OmniRoute on the controller The role ships a tree; it does not fetch one. The build host clones it for itself, so it needs to be reachable from the guest. The build host provisioned appctl install builder. The build cannot run on the controller and must not run emulated. 24 GB of RAM on the Proxmox host The build's webpack process reaches 11.5 GB RSS. The builder role asserts this and refuses a host that is too small.

SSH access means whatever your SSH setup already provides. The framework does not read ~/.ssh/config by name, and it does not need one. If you keep your hosts in an SSH config, name the host in the inventory and the alias resolves on its own:

all:
  children:
    proxmox:
      hosts:
        pve:
          ansible_host: pve.example.net   # a Host block in ~/.ssh/config
          ansible_user: root

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Report a vulnerability privately rather than in a public issue.

Use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting on this repository, or email the maintainer. Please include the version or commit, the target you were using (proxmox_lxc is the only implemented one), and the steps that reproduce it.

What to expect: an acknowledgement, then a fix or an explanation of why the report is not a vulnerability.

docs.title: What this tool does and does not protect
docs.text:
• Secrets live in a gitignored .env, mode 0600. They reach Ansible in a mode-0600 extra-vars file, never in argv, so they do not appear in ps. The tool redacts password-shaped values from the logs it writes, but that is a best effort against a known set of shapes, not a guarantee.
  • The guest's SSH host key is trusted on first contact (accept-new). The proxmox_lxc target removes a stale known_hosts entry for an address it has just created, because a DHCP lease can hand an old address to a new container.
  • The Proxmox host is reached over SSH and needs permission to run pct. The tool does not manage that permission.
