docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
How appctl fits together. Read ../README.md for why it is built this way and ../AGENTS.md before changing it.

  • Data flow — one end-to-end run
  • Modules — what owns what
  • Why the boundary — the rule and its consequences
  • Extension points — where a change belongs
  • Invariants — what must stay true

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text:
What happens when you run appctl install. One question per diagram: what happens, in order; then where a secret goes.

Hold "Alt" / "Option" to enable pan & zoom 
flowchart TD
    CFG["app.yaml<br/>the one configuration file"]
    LOAD["config.load<br/>parse and validate"]

    SEC{{"secrets check<br/>required keys present in .env ?"}}
    STOP["STOP — names the missing keys<br/>before anything is touched"]

    RENDER["render<br/>YAML to JSON on this laptop"]
    OUT["tmp/rendered/app/config.json"]

    VARS["one temp JSON, mode 0600<br/>secrets and rendered config paths"]
    ANS["ansible-playbook -vvv<br/>extra-vars from the file, never argv"]

    PLAY1["PLAY 1 — common/lxc<br/>pct create, discover the DHCP lease"]
    PLAY2["PLAY 2 — apps/app<br/>install, configure, start"]

    LOGS["tmp/runs/TIMESTAMP/<br/>commands.txt log.txt recap.txt errors.txt"]

    CFG --> LOAD
    LOAD --> SEC
    SEC -->|no| STOP
    SEC -->|yes| RENDER
    RENDER --> OUT
    OUT --> VARS
    SEC --> VARS
    VARS --> ANS
    ANS --> PLAY1
    PLAY1 --> PLAY2
    PLAY2 --> LOGS

    classDef fail fill:#fde8e8,stroke:#c0392b
    classDef file fill:#eef4ff,stroke:#4a6fa5
    class STOP fail
    class CFG,OUT,VARS,LOGS file

Three things are worth noticing.

Nothing for configuration runs on the guest. render happens on your laptop. The play copies a finished file. An application needs no code of its own to be configured.

The extra-vars file is flat. --extra-vars @file does not unwrap an ansible: key; that namespace is a config-file convention. A wrapped file is accepted without complaint and defines nothing, so every secret arrives empty while the controller holds good values. Measured both ways.

Rendered-config paths travel in the same file as the secrets rather than on the command line. They are controller paths and harmless, and keeping the whole variable set in one place means one file to delete.

docs.title: Where a secret goes
docs.text:
appctl install is the same command, followed through time. The value crosses three boundaries and never reaches a log.

Hold "Alt" / "Option" to enable pan & zoom 
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant OP as "Operator"
    participant LC as "appctl"
    participant ENV as ".env on the laptop"
    participant ANS as "ansible-playbook"
    participant GUEST as "The guest"
    participant APP as "The application"

    OP->>LC: appctl secrets set NAME value
    LC->>ENV: write, mode 0600, gitignored
    Note over ENV: the only place the value exists in plain text

    OP->>LC: appctl install
    LC->>ENV: read
    ENV-->>LC: the values
    LC->>LC: fail here if a required one is unset
    LC->>ANS: extra-vars from a temp 0600 file
    Note right of ANS: never in argv, so never visible in ps

    ANS->>GUEST: write the EnvironmentFile, mode 0600, owned by root
    GUEST->>APP: start the unit
    APP->>APP: resolve dollar-brace NAME from the EnvironmentFile

    Note over LC,APP: the value crosses three boundaries and never enters a log

In a rendered config file a secret appears only as a dollar-brace NAME reference, which the guest resolves at startup. That is what makes a config file safe to commit.

appctl build is a separate path and does not appear above: it produces the wheel and the lockfile that the play later installs. See build-pipeline.md.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
Module Owns Knows about applications? config.py the schema of app.yaml and nothing else no targets/ where and how an application runs no — a target is not an application secrets.py .env parsing, writing, checking no render.py YAML → JSON with {{ }} substitution no build.py wheel + lockfile from a git checkout no — a repo is a repo install.py running Ansible, streaming, redaction no state.py writes the state: block into app.yaml, as text no cli.py argument parsing, dispatch, exit codes no errors.py the exception hierarchy no

Dependencies flow one way. cli depends on everything. install and render depend on config. Nothing depends on build except cli. There is no import cycle and no module imports two others for convenience.

config.py knows the three source kinds — package, repo, toolchain — because the schema has to accept all three. It knows nothing about any of them beyond whether they have an artifact, because a kind that had a per-application behaviour would put the application in the framework.

docs.title: Why config.py is the centre
docs.text: Every other module needs the same three things: which applications exist, where the repository root is, and what each one requires. That is Config. Parsing it in one place, with one strictness policy, means a typo in app.yaml fails once and names the key — rather than surfacing later as a service listening on the wrong port.

docs.title: Why the boundary holds
docs.text:
The repository is split into two role roots:

common/   the framework — names no application
apps/     one directory per application

src/appctl/ sits on the framework side. The boundary is not decorative: it is what makes adding an application safe.

The cost. Some things that would be convenient are unavailable. The tool cannot pre-check that an application's unit name is correct, cannot know that example-app needs two ports, cannot offer a --example-app flag. Each of those would be a piece of the framework that knows about an application, and the second application needing the same thing would turn it into either a duplicate or a conflict.

The benefit. Adding an application cannot break an existing one, because nothing shared changed. apps/example-app and apps/another coexist with no shared code beyond the contract, and each derives every path from app_name.

The app_name clause in the contract follows from the same rule. The framework declares no default for it, because a role's meta dependency has its defaults applied after the including role's own — so a framework default would silently override the application's. That was masked while there was one application, because its name happened to equal the default.

docs.title: Extension points
docs.text:
Where a change belongs:

You want to… Put it in configure an application differently apps/<app>/config.yml and its app.yaml config: block install a different artifact apps/<app>/ and the source: block require another secret the secrets: list in app.yaml change how guests are created common/lxc/ support another delivery target src/appctl/targets/ — see targets.md change the venv contract common/python/ add an application apps/<app>/ — see the deployflow-add-app skill add a appctl command src/appctl/cli.py plus a new module teach the tool an application name nowhere. Put it in apps/.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
These must hold. Each was a real failure before it became a rule.

A secret never reaches a log. Ansible echoes extra variables back at -vvv from two places: the argument vector and its own extra_vars: output. install.py rewrites both. Verify:

appctl install <app> -- -e some_secret=PLAINTEXTVALUE
grep -rl PLAINTEXTVALUE tmp/        # must print nothing

A second run reports changed=0. A role that reports a change on every run is reinstalling itself, which tells you nothing about its own state. The usual cause is a sentinel that can never succeed — it looks like a guard and silently holds a gate open. 'changed' in "unchanged" is True; an import of a name that does not exist always fails; a glob read by next() twice raises StopIteration.

An unknown key in app.yaml is an error. A misspelled key is otherwise a silent no-op.

An unimplemented target fails before any side effect. A manifest that names vm or docker_vm is refused while nothing has been built, downloaded or started. The registry never falls back to proxmox_lxc: an application that asks for a virtual machine must not be silently installed into a container.

The shared code names no target. pct, the container ID, the template and the guest network live in targets/proxmox_lxc.py. A module outside targets/ that mentions one of them is in the wrong place.

A record is written to app.yaml after every build and install, and only the state: block is rewritten — never the whole file, because a YAML round-trip destroys the comments that explain why each value is what it is.

Run logs are never pruned. appctl deletes exactly one file: the temporary extra-vars file. Everything under tmp/runs/ survives.

appctl install X also runs the lxc tag. Play 1 is what discovers the DHCP lease. Without it play 2 cannot resolve the guest at all. It is guarded by a stat, so on an existing guest it costs a few no-op tasks.

A toolchain role declares no dependency on common/python. That dependency asserts app_port is defined, and a build host serves nothing. A role with no dependency still runs, because play 2 loops over each host's app_roles and include_roles it — so the exemption costs no playbook change. What it does cost is the framework's derived paths: a toolchain defines what it needs.

A toolchain's role asserts the machine, not the install. The minimums are measured. A builder sized at 12 GB passed every install check and then failed during a build with an error naming a memory limit rather than the guest — and the guest stopped answering SSH. A role that installs a compiler and reports success has not said anything about whether a build can run on it.

docs.title: Build pipeline
docs.text: How appctl build turns a git checkout into the two artifacts a role installs, and which of them is committed.

docs.title: What it produces
docs.text:
apps/<app>/files/
  requirements.lock        sha256-pinned dependency tree      COMMITTED
  dist/
    <app>-<version>-py3-none-any.whl                          gitignored
    BUILDINFO                fork, commit, wheel sha256        gitignored

The split is deliberate. The lockfile is committed because it is a pure function of the checkout's pyproject.toml, so a diff of it means something and a reviewer can read it. The wheel is not, because it is a multi-megabyte binary that changes on every commit, and BUILDINFO records the sha256 that makes it verifiable. Committing it would buy nothing BUILDINFO does not already say.

BUILDINFO is YAML, because the role reads it with from_yaml. An earlier key=value format parsed as a bare scalar and failed with dictionary update sequence element #0 has length 1; 2 is required.

Values that could parse as something other than a string are quoted: python_target: "3.14". Unquoted it reads as a float, and the role asserts it equals the string "3.14".

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1  fetch            optional, --fetch
 2  resolve ref      tag, branch or sha → a commit
 3  assert clean     refuse a dirty checkout
 4  export           git archive → a throwaway tree, no .git
 5  seed commit      write _build_commit.txt into the tree
 6  build webui      bun install --frozen-lockfile && bun run build
 7  build wheel      uv build --wheel
 8  verify commit    ask the wheel which commit it is
 9  compile lock     uv pip compile from the checkout's pyproject.toml
10  verify hashes    every entry must carry a sha256
11  publish          copy into files/, write BUILDINFO

The build happens in a temp directory from git archive, never in your checkout. Step 6 writes hundreds of packages into webui/node_modules and step 7 writes into example-app/web/dist; neither belongs in a tree you also edit.

docs.title: The three checks, and why each exists
docs.text:
Each of these exists because a build can quietly produce an artifact that lies.

A dirty checkout is refused. The wheel records a commit sha. Built from a dirty tree, that sha describes code that was never pushed and cannot be reproduced by anyone else — the provenance would be false. Step 8 then asks the wheel which commit it is, rather than asking the checkout, so the application states its own provenance rather than having it asserted for it.

Every lock entry must carry a sha256. The guest installs with --require-hashes, which fails the whole install if one entry lacks a hash. Checked here, the error names the package. At install time, pip names nothing.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
The same commit produces a byte-identical wheel. Measured:

$ appctl build example-app && sha256sum apps/example-app/files/dist/*.whl
7cf11926d6329554810538f751e3d6f5dca0f6e265179350710e6f0de2c2a004

Rebuilt on a later day from the same commit, the same sha256. That is what makes BUILDINFO a meaningful check rather than a record.

docs.title: One change after every build
docs.text:
BUILDINFO carries a built: timestamp, so rebuilding it changes its content and the play copies it again — one task reports changed on the first run after a build. The second run settles to changed=0.

That is correct rather than noisy: the record genuinely is new. Use appctl build <app> --check when you want to verify without churning it.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
appctl build <app>                # build
appctl build <app> --check        # verify committed artifacts, build nothing
appctl build <app> --dry-run      # resolve the ref and stop
appctl build <app> --ref v1.2     # override source.ref
appctl build <app> --fetch        # git fetch first

--check is the cheap one. It reports the lockfile's package count, whether every entry carries a sha256, and the recorded fork commit and wheel sha256, without building. Run it before deploying to see whether the artifacts on disk are the ones a build would produce.

docs.title: What the role checks
docs.text:
Before installing anything, the role re-reads the sha256 from BUILDINFO and compares it against the wheel that landed on the guest. That check exists because a truncated copy and a rebuilt wheel both look like a successful copy.

It then confirms the installed package reports the expected commit — read out of the installed code, because that is the thing which will run.

docs.title: When an application needs no build
docs.text:
source.kind: package means the wheel already exists on PyPI. appctl build exits non-zero and says so:

error: example-app is installed from bottle==0.13.3, so there is nothing to build

That is deliberate. Silently succeeding would hide a misconfiguration where someone expected a build and the version was never pinned.

A toolchain source says the same thing for a third reason. It installs nothing from anywhere — it is the environment another application is built in — so there is no artifact to produce and nothing to fetch:

error: builder is a toolchain guest, so there is nothing to build

its role assembles the environment itself; run `appctl install builder` to provision it

See configuration.md for what a toolchain source is and why it is not one of the other two kinds.

docs.title: The other build path: a tree built on a build host
docs.text:
appctl build produces a Python artifact — a wheel and a pinned lockfile. That is the right shape for a Python application and the wrong shape for everything else.

A Node tree of the kind OmniRoute is cannot be moved to the guest as a wheel, and it cannot be built on the controller either. The controller is arm64 macOS and the guest is x86_64 Linux, so a tree built on the controller carries darwin-only native binaries — sharp-darwin-arm64, @esbuild/darwin-arm64 — that fail on the guest much later, as an unrelated error deep in a request handler.

And an emulated container is not the answer. It gets the architecture right and then falls over twice over:

Failure Cause Next.js build worker exited with code: null and signal: SIGKILL at ~5.6 GB the emulated process sees the VM's memory, not the container's limit fatal error: receive on synctest channel from outside bubble / SIGSEGV esbuild is a Go binary, and the Go runtime faults under qemu. No amount of memory fixes this.

So the build runs on a native x86_64 host, and that host is a guest this repository provisions:

appctl install builder                        # the build host
apps/omniroute/build/omr-build-linux.sh   /path/to/OmniRoute main                     # the build
appctl install omniroute                      # ship it

Three things about that path are worth knowing, because each one is a rule the framework could not have taught an agent by itself:

The build host clones the repository itself. A transferred tree has no .git, so git rev-parse --short HEAD does not resolve and the artifact carries no provenance. And a tar of a macOS checkout carries AppleDouble sidecars (._aliasConfig.ts and hundreds like it) that esbuild reads as source files and rejects with Unexpected "\x00".

The clone is pinned to a commit, not to a branch. git clone --branch main resolves main at clone time, and main moves. A push between the controller reading HEAD and the builder cloning produces an artifact whose receipt does not name the commit that was asked for — which defeats the check the receipt exists to satisfy.

The build writes a receipt, and the role refuses rather than rebuilds. A role that rebuilds on every play cannot tell "no changes" from "rebuilt". The receipt records the commit, the version and the platform, and the role refuses to ship a tree whose receipt does not match the checkout.

The build host is itself an application — a toolchain — so it is provisioned, asserted and version-controlled like any other. See apps/builder/ and apps/omniroute/docs/BUILDING-FROM-SOURCE.md.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
The full shape of app.yaml. The repository README has the short version; this is the one to check a key against.

Unknown keys are an error. The tool rejects any key not listed here, naming the key and where it was found. A misspelled key would otherwise be dropped, and a silently dropped key is how a service comes up on the wrong port.

docs.title: Top level
docs.text:
version: 1              # integer
defaults: {...}         # guest shape, inherited by every application
applications: {...}     # the applications

docs.title: defaults
docs.text:
defaults:
  python_version: "3.14"                              # quoted; unquoted is a float
  template: ubuntu-26.04-standard_26.04-1_amd64.tar.zst
  storage: data1
  rootfs_gb: 16
  cores: 2
  memory_mb: 2048
  swap_mb: 512
  features: nesting=1,fuse=1,keyctl=1
  onboot: 0

Every key has a default, so defaults: may be omitted entirely.

docs.title: applications.<name>
docs.text:
applications:
  <name>:
    description: one line, shown by `appctl list`   # optional
    target:     {...}                               # required
    source:     {...}                               # required
    build:      {...}                               # required when source.kind is repo
    config:     {...}                               # optional
    secrets:    [NAME, ...]                         # optional

name is the key. It must match the directory name under apps/, because the role is looked up by it.

docs.title: target
docs.text:
target:
  kind: proxmox_lxc         # required: the target that runs this application
  options:                  # optional: the target's own settings
    hostname: example-app-ansible
    vmid: 117               # optional; omit and the role skips create
    bind_host: 0.0.0.0      # default 127.0.0.1

kind names a registered target. proxmox_lxc is the only one implemented; vm and docker_vm are planned and fail before anything is built. See targets.md.

options belongs to the target. The shared schema does not read inside it, so a new target never changes config.py. A misspelled key under options is caught by the target, not by this schema.

For proxmox_lxc there is deliberately no address field. A guest takes a DHCP lease from Proxmox's SDN zone and common/lxc reads the address back. An ip: key is rejected. This is not caution: a statically addressed Ubuntu 26.04 guest comes up with no IPv4 at all, an empty /etc/netplan/, and systemd-networkd exiting 243/CREDENTIALS, and apt cannot resolve. Verified on a live container.

docs.title: source
docs.text:
Three kinds, because they describe genuinely different things. What differs is not the value of kind but what has to happen before the application can be installed.

Kind The code comes from Has an artifact? appctl build package a published version yes — it already exists exits non-zero: nothing to build repo a commit in a checkout no — it has to be built builds it toolchain nowhere — the application is the environment no exits non-zero: nothing to build 
# published on PyPI — nothing to build
source:
  kind: package
  package: "myapp[browser]==1.2.3"    # required when kind is package

# built from a checkout — wheel plus pinned lockfile
source:
  kind: repo                          # required
  repo: /path/to/checkout             # required when kind is repo
  ref: HEAD                           # default HEAD
  output: dist                        # default dist, relative to files/
  webui: {...}                        # optional, see below

# nothing is installed from anywhere — the application IS the environment
source:
  kind: toolchain                     # required

appctl build <name> on a package source exits non-zero and says there is nothing to build. That is deliberate: silently succeeding would hide a misconfiguration.

docs.title: kind: repo
docs.text:
The build: block is required for this kind and the tool rejects a repo source without one, naming the omission. It describes a Python build — a wheel plus a pinned lockfile — and that is what appctl build produces.

An application built from a source checkout in another language does not use appctl build. It has its own build script, because the build has to run on the platform the artifact targets and the tree is far too large to move around. apps/omniroute/ is the worked example: its build: block is deliberately inert, and the real build is apps/omniroute/build/omr-build-linux.sh. See build-pipeline.md.

docs.title: kind: toolchain
docs.text:
A toolchain application installs no service and publishes no port. Its role assembles the environment another application is built in — a compiler, a pinned runtime, a workspace — and then stops.

It exists because the alternative is to describe that environment as one of the other two kinds, and both are lies:

  • package claims something is installed from a registry. Nothing is.
  • repo claims there is a checkout to build. There is not one; and the schema requires a build: block for a repo source, so the manifest would carry a block that does nothing.

So a toolchain source has no package, no repo and no build: block, and appctl build on it says there is nothing to build for the same reason a package does.

The role for a toolchain has no dependency on common/python, and that is load-bearing rather than a style choice: common/python asserts that app_port is defined, and a builder serves nothing. A role with no dependency still runs — play 2 of playbooks/site.yml loops over each host's app_roles and include_roles it — so nothing in the playbook changes.

The builder application in this repository is the worked example. Its postconditions assert the properties a build depends on rather than the exit codes of the install commands, and it publishes its address to tmp/builders/<name>.endpoint so the build script can find it: guest hostnames do not resolve from the controller, because Proxmox's resolver is not the controller's.

The minimums are measured, not guessed. A builder sized at 12 GB passed every install check and then failed during a build, with an error that named a memory limit rather than the guest — and the guest stopped answering SSH entirely. The role asserts the floor it needs, so a guest resized by hand is checked at install time rather than discovered during a build.

See apps/builder/ for the working role.

docs.title: source.webui
docs.text:
Only for an application with a frontend.

webui:
  path: webui                   # required, relative to the exported tree
  package_manager: auto         # auto | bun | npm — default auto
  build_command: build          # default build
  install_command: null         # null picks bun --frozen-lockfile or npm ci

The bundle is built before the wheel so the wheel carries it and the guest never needs Node.

docs.title: build
docs.text:
Required when source.kind is repo; the tool rejects a repo source without one, naming the omission.

build:
  python_version: "3.14"    # default: defaults.python_version
  lock_requirement: null    # null compiles the checkout's own pyproject.toml
  ref: null                 # overrides source.ref
  fetch: false              # git fetch before resolving ref
  verify_lock: true         # refuse a lock entry with no sha256

lock_requirement: null is the normal case. It compiles from the checkout's own pyproject.toml so the tree tracks the fork, rather than from a PyPI release that may lag it.

docs.title: config
docs.text:
Renders YAML on the controller. See rendering.md.

config:
  target: "{{ app_state_dir }}/config.json"   # required
  files: [apps/<name>/config.yml]             # required; a string is accepted
  mode: "0640"                                # default 0640
  vars:                                       # optional, values keep their type
    port: 9000

target is resolved by Ansible, so a {{ }} expression there is fine. vars values keep the type YAML gives them: port: 9000 is an integer, and a whole-value {{ port }} renders the integer.

docs.title: secrets
docs.text:
Names of keys required in .env before this application can be installed.

secrets:
  - myapp_provider_api_key
  - myapp_webui_token_secret

appctl install refuses to start while any of them is unset, and names the missing ones. See secrets.md.

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text:
app.yaml says an application exists; the inventory says it is deployed. The two are separate, and appctl reports them separately.

An application is deployed when its name appears in an app_roles list under inventory/group_vars/*/main.yml:

# inventory/group_vars/ex/main.yml
app_roles:
  - example-app

The inventory is gitignored — it holds your own hosts — so a fresh clone has none. Create it from inventory.example/; the skill (.agents/skills/deployflow-add-app/SKILL.md) has the full procedure.

appctl list shows that in the DEPLOYED column. Selection follows from it:

The name is positional: appctl install example-app. Flags follow it, and anything after a bare -- goes to ansible-playbook.

Situation What appctl install does example-app, deployed installs it example-app, not deployed refuses, says to add it to app_roles no name, exactly one deployed installs that one no name, several deployed refuses and prints the exact commands no name, none deployed refuses

Secrets are checked for the selected applications only. That is the point of requiring a selection: with N applications, demanding every secret up front means one application you are not deploying can block the one you are.

docs.title: state — written by the tool
docs.text:
Never hand-edit. A build or an install writes it:

state:
  built:
    commit: "a27f294f52293c476ff8ccc546439be203b066ca"
    wheel_sha256: "7cf11926d6329554810538f751e3d6f5dca0f6e265179350710e6f0de2c2a004"
    packages: 96
    at: "2026-10-11T11:58:31Z"
  installed:
    at: "2026-10-11T11:58:14Z"
    changed: 0
    failed: 0
    tasks: 71
    seconds: 40

An install is recorded whether it passed or failed. Only built and installed are accepted; anything else is rejected, because the next write would drop it silently.

The file is edited as text, not loaded and re-dumped: app.yaml carries 18 comment lines and a PyYAML round-trip destroys every one. Only the state: block is rewritten. See ../src/appctl/state.py.

The trade: a timestamp in a committed file is a diff on every run. That is what a record is, but it is churn in review.

docs.title: Substitutions in rendered files
docs.text:
Two syntaxes, and the difference is the point:

{{ name }} substituted by appctl on the controller, from config.vars plus the built-ins below ${NAME} left exactly as written, resolved by the application at runtime from its EnvironmentFile

Built-ins: app_name, app_home, app_dir, app_state_dir. The three paths mirror common/python/defaults/main.yml. Anything else must be declared under config.vars.

A placeholder occupying a whole value keeps its declared type. A placeholder inside a longer string is always a string, because concatenation is what it means:

port: "{{ api_port }}"                  # → 8900   (an int)
workspace: "{{ app_state_dir }}/work"    # → "/opt/myapp/state/work"

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Everything is checked at load, before any command does work:

Problem Message misspelled key unknown key in applications.x: <key> repo source with no build <app> has source.kind: repo but no build block missing guest.hostname applications.x.guest.hostname is required webui with no path applications.x.source.webui.path is required unparseable YAML the YAML error, with its line number

appctl list shows what was parsed, which is the quickest way to confirm a file was read the way you meant it.

docs.title: DeployFlow — reference
docs.text:
This is the reference for the current implementation: the appctl command, the Proxmox LXC target, the manifest and the Ansible roles.

For what the workflow is and why you would point an agent at it, read the project README. Start with that one.

Deploy applications to Proxmox LXC containers with Ansible, then verify the service works — not just that the deployment command succeeded.

The tool is appctl. It builds a pinned artifact, installs it into a guest, and then runs checks that reach the application the way a user does.

appctl targets                     # what can be delivered to, and what cannot yet
appctl list                        # what is configured
appctl build example-app           # produce the artifacts the role installs
appctl install example-app         # install it and check that it answers
appctl secrets check               # are the required secrets set?

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
A stock Ubuntu template goes in, Ansible configures it, and the application runs under systemd with a sha256-pinned dependency tree. No container image is built, so there is no tarball to store and no image registry in the loop.

Install a pinned application into a Proxmox LXC guest, with Ansible Reproducibility the lockfile carries a hash for every dependency; the build refuses one that does not Verification application-level checks after the install, not only a green playbook Secrets in a gitignored .env, passed to Ansible in a mode-0600 file, never in argv Build hosts a build host is an application too — a toolchain, provisioned and asserted like any other

docs.title: Why the checks matter
docs.text:
Ansible reporting success proves that Ansible ran. It does not prove the application is usable. Each of these passed review and only failed in use:

The check What it catches The package imports A dependency tree that did not install The unit is active A service systemd accepted and then dropped The port is listening A process that bound somewhere other than the requested port The endpoint answers A service that listens and returns nothing

Every application role carries its own checks, because only the application knows what "working" means for it. The sample role in apps/example-app/ shows the pattern.

docs.title: The three kinds of application
docs.text:
A manifest says where an application's code comes from. There are three kinds, and they differ in more than the value of source.kind — they differ in what has to happen before the application can be installed.

Kind Source Has an artifact? appctl build package a published version yes — it already exists exits non-zero: nothing to build repo a commit in a checkout no — it has to be built builds it toolchain nothing no — it is the environment exits non-zero: nothing to build

A toolchain is an application whose purpose is to be the environment another application is built in. It installs no service, publishes no port, and has no artifact. Its role assembles what a build needs and asserts the machine can build:

builder:
  description: the guest other applications are built on
  target:
  source:
    kind: toolchain
  secrets: []

Three things follow from it being a toolchain, and each is deliberate:

No dependency on common/python. That dependency is what asserts app_port is defined, and a build host serves nothing. A role with no dependency still runs — play 2 loops over each host's app_roles and include_roles it — so no playbook changes.

The postconditions are about the machine, not the install. A role that installs a compiler and reports success has not said anything about whether a build can run on it. The builder asserts the architecture, the pinned runtime, the memory, the disk and the registry's reachability.

The minimums are measured, not guessed. A builder created with 12 GB of RAM passed every install check and then failed during a build, with an error naming a memory limit rather than the guest — and the guest stopped answering SSH entirely. The role now refuses a guest below the floor it needs.

The two shipped applications that need a build are the two hard shapes:

Application Shape What it shows apps/omniroute/ repo — built from a checkout a source build that refuses a stale tree, and checks an inference plane's key gate apps/builder/ toolchain a guest that exists to build the other one

Two more need no build at all: apps/example-app/ is a small HTTP service that installs from a pinned wheel, and apps/omniroute-release/ installs a published npm release.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
A target says where and how an application runs. The manifest names one:

applications:
  example-app:
    target:
      kind: proxmox_lxc
      options:
        hostname: example-app
        vmid: 121

proxmox_lxc is the only implemented target. Two more are planned:

Target What it would do Status vm Provision a virtual machine and install the application into it planned docker_vm Provision a virtual machine and run the application in Docker there planned

A manifest that names an unimplemented target fails before it builds, downloads or starts anything:

error: target kind 'vm' is planned but not implemented

provision a virtual machine and install the application into it.
implemented targets: proxmox_lxc

That failure is deliberate. An application that asks for a virtual machine must not be silently installed into a container instead.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
You need a Proxmox VE host, a cached Linux template on it, and SSH access to the host.

git clone https://github.com/bruj0/deployflow.git
cd deployflow

uv tool install --editable .

cp app.example.yaml app.yaml        # then edit it

# The inventory is gitignored — it names your own hosts — so a fresh clone
# has none. Create it from the committed templates.
mkdir -p inventory/group_vars
cp inventory.example/hosts.yml inventory/hosts.yml
cp -r inventory.example/group_vars/. inventory/group_vars/

Edit three things:

  1. app.yaml — the application, its port and its target options.
  2. inventory/hosts.yml — your Proxmox host and the guest.
  3. inventory/group_vars/all/main.yml — your SSH public key.

inventory/ stays out of git on purpose: it names your Proxmox host, the guest IDs and the addresses of machines only you can reach. Nothing in it is a credential, and none of it is public either. The committed templates in inventory.example/ show the shape of every key.

Then:

appctl secrets init                  # create .env from the required keys
appctl secrets set NAME 'value'      # add each secret
appctl secrets check                 # confirm they are all set
appctl render                        # see the configuration before it lands
appctl install example-app

Run the install a second time. It should report changed=0: the same inputs produce the same guest.

docs.title: What an application role owes the framework
docs.text:
An application is one directory under apps/. Nothing in common/ or playbooks/ changes when you add one.

# apps/myapp/defaults/main.yml
app_name: myapp        # the only required value
app_port: 9000

# apps/myapp/meta/main.yml
dependencies:
  - role: python       # declares the dependency, so no playbook changes

app_name derives the service account, the directories, the virtual environment and the unit name. app_port has no derivation and you must set it.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
app.yaml                 the one configuration file: applications and targets
common/                  framework. Names no application, anywhere.
  lxc/                   pct create from a stock template, DHCP, address discovery
  python/                toolchain, service account, venv — the contract
apps/                    one directory per application
  example-app/           the sample used by the quickstart
  omniroute/             OmniRoute, built from a source checkout
    build/               the build script and its host-side half
    docs/                what building it taught
  omniroute-release/     OmniRoute, installed from a published npm release
  builder/               a toolchain: the guest other applications are built on
src/appctl/              the appctl package
  targets/               the delivery-target interface and its implementations
    proxmox_lxc.py       the only implemented target
docs/                    architecture, configuration, rendering, secrets, build
playbooks/site.yml
inventory/               guests; the only file you edit to add one.
                         GITIGNORED — it names your own hosts. Create it
                         from inventory.example/.
inventory.example/       the committed templates for the above

roles_path = common:apps. A role's meta dependency declares what it needs, so adding an application never edits a playbook.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command What it does appctl list Every application, its target, its destination and its last install appctl targets The implemented targets, and the planned ones that are not built appctl init Write a starting app.yaml appctl build <app> Produce the artifacts the role installs appctl build --check Verify the committed artifacts and build nothing appctl render Render the application configuration, without deploying appctl install <app> Install it and run the checks appctl secrets init\|set\|list\|check Manage the .env

Anything after a bare -- goes straight to ansible-playbook:

appctl install example-app -- --check --diff

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text: How an application's YAML configuration becomes the file the guest reads, and why there is no per-application code.

docs.title: The path
docs.text:
Hold "Alt" / "Option" to enable pan & zoom 
flowchart TD
    YAML["apps/app/config.yml<br/>committed"]
    RENDER["appctl render<br/>substitutes double-brace names"]
    JSON["tmp/rendered/app/config.json<br/>not committed, not secret"]
    VARS["passed to Ansible as<br/>appctl_rendered_configs"]
    COPY["common/python<br/>copies it"]
    TARGET["/opt/app/state/config.json<br/>the application reads it"]

    YAML --> RENDER
    RENDER --> JSON
    JSON --> VARS
    VARS --> COPY
    COPY --> TARGET

    classDef file fill:#eef4ff,stroke:#4a6fa5
    class YAML,JSON file

docs.title: The file is partial, on purpose
docs.text:
An application merges its own defaults into whatever it is given. example-app does this in example-app/config/loader.py:178:

def merge_missing_defaults(existing, defaults):
    """Recursively add missing defaults without replacing configured values."""

It ships its own minimal render-config.json for its Render.com deployment, which is the same idea: write what differs, let the application fill the rest.

Verified on a live guest — a two-key file boots the service:

{ "gateway": { "port": 18790 },
  "providers": { "anthropic": { "apiKey": "${EXAMPLE_APP_API_KEY}" } } }

{"status": "ok", "process": "alive", "ready": true, "websocket": "running"}

So a rendered file with three keys is a normal, complete result. Not a degraded one.

docs.title: Why there is no per-application script
docs.text:
There was one. apps/example-app/files/example-app-configure.py merged settings into config.json on the guest every play. It was 112 lines, took nine positional arguments, and reimplemented merge_missing_defaults in Python.

It was removed because it was a second implementation of behaviour the application already had, shipped to every guest, free to drift from it — and because it ran on the guest at install time for no benefit. The application does the merge. That is strictly better, and the reason it was not obvious is that the merge script predated the discovery that the application does it.

Do not add one. If an application needs something rendered that its own loader cannot fill in, that belongs in the YAML.

docs.title: Substitutions
docs.text:
# {{ name }}   substituted here, on the controller
port: "{{ api_port }}"
workspace: "{{ app_state_dir }}/workspace"

# ${NAME}      left exactly as written
apiKey: "${EXAMPLE_APP_API_KEY}"

The split is the safety property. A ${NAME} reference is safe to commit; the value is resolved on the guest, from a 0600 root-owned EnvironmentFile, at startup. Unifying the two would resolve secrets here and write them to a file.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
A placeholder occupying a whole value keeps the type it was declared with:

# config.vars:  api_port: 8900
api: { port: "{{ api_port }}" }      →  8900        an integer

A placeholder inside a longer string is always a string, because concatenation is what it means:

workspace: "{{ app_state_dir }}/workspace"   →  "/opt/example-app/state/workspace"

Both were wrong at some point during development — flattening everything to str rendered "8900", which some applications reject.

docs.title: What is available
docs.text:
Name Source app_name the key in applications: app_home, app_dir, app_state_dir derived from app_name anything in config.vars declared by the application

An undefined name is an error naming the file and the placeholder. It is not left as literal text, because a config that renders differently on two runs is worse than one that does not render.

The three paths mirror common/python/defaults/main.yml, which creates them. That is a deliberate duplication: appctl has to know where the state directory is to render a config into it, and common/python has to create it. Two places that must agree is only safe if something makes them agree.

docs.title: Multiple files
docs.text:
config.files accepts a list. Later files merge over earlier ones, key by key:

config:
  files:
    - apps/myapp/config.yml        # the base
    - apps/myapp/production.yml    # overrides

docs.title: Reviewing before deploying
docs.text:
appctl render writes the file and stops. Read it — it is exactly what the guest will get:

appctl render
cat tmp/rendered/<app>/config.json

It is not committed and not secret, because it contains only ${NAME} references.

docs.title: Where the file lands
docs.text:
app_config_target in the role's defaults/main.yml decides:

app_config_target: "{{ app_state_dir }}/config.json"

common/python copies it there as app_user, mode 0640. It registers the result as app_rendered_config, which an application can use to restart its units only when the file actually changed:

when: app_rendered_config.changed | default(false)

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: Where a secret lives, how it travels, and the three places it can leak.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
The full path of a value is drawn as a sequence diagram in architecture.md. In short:

Where State .env on the laptop the only plain-text copy, mode 0600, gitignored the temp extra-vars file mode 0600, passed as --extra-vars @file, deleted at exit the guest's EnvironmentFile mode 0600, owned by root the application's memory resolved from that file at startup any log never — see the three leaks

A secret is never written to app.yaml, to a rendered config file, or to a log. In a config file it appears only as a ${NAME} reference, which the guest resolves at startup. That is what makes a config file safe to commit.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
appctl secrets init              # writes .env (0600) and .env.example
appctl secrets check             # what is set; exit 1 while anything required is missing
appctl secrets list              # names and state, never values
appctl secrets set NAME 'value'  # positional
appctl secrets set NAME          # prompts, value never in argv or shell history
appctl secrets set NAME --generate

set rewrites the file in place, preserving existing keys and their order, so running it twice for one key leaves one entry. A duplicate KEY in a .env file is a well-known source of "I changed it and nothing happened".

Values needing spaces or # are quoted automatically. Read them back with dotenv if you need to.

docs.title: Why not ansible-vault
docs.text:
The vault file this repository used was encrypted with a throwaway password that was then deleted. It became undecryptable and unrecoverable from the repository, and every run failed at:

[ERROR]: Attempting to decrypt but no vault secrets found

A secret store you can permanently lock yourself out of is a worse default than a plain file that is simply not committed. The trade is real: .env has no second factor. That is why it is mode 0600, gitignored, and why .env.example — the list of required keys, with no values — is committed, so a fresh clone knows what to fill in.

Do not reintroduce a vault without a password the operator actually holds.

docs.title: The three leaks, and the guards
1. In argv
docs.text:
An extra variable passed as -e key=value is visible in ps for the whole run, to every process on the machine.

Guard. Secrets go in a mode-0600 temporary file passed as --extra-vars @file. The file is deleted when the run ends, including on failure.

docs.title: 2. In Ansible's own echo
docs.text:
Measured. At -vvv, a secret passed as an extra variable appears twice:

extra_vars: ('myapp_api_key=PLAINTEXT',)      # Ansible echoing our own argv
...
"myapp_api_key": "PLAINTEXT"                  # and the value in the result

no_log: true censors a task that opts in, at any verbosity. It does not protect a secret passed as an ordinary variable — the protection is per-task, not global.

Guard. install.py rewrites both before anything reaches a file: the argv it logs, and the extra_vars: line as it streams. Filtering our own argv is not enough on its own; the value comes back a second time from Ansible.

Verify after any change to the streaming code:

appctl install myapp -- -e some_secret=PLAINTEXTVALUE
grep -rl PLAINTEXTVALUE tmp/          # must print nothing

docs.title: 3. In a rendered config
docs.text:
A rendered config.json is written under tmp/rendered/, which is gitignored — but a secret in it would still be a secret on disk in plain text, and would be copied to the guest.

Guard. The renderer substitutes {{ name }} and leaves ${NAME} alone. Collapsing the two would resolve a secret here and write it to a file. Keep them distinct.

docs.title: Generating versus providing
docs.text:
--generate uses secrets.token_urlsafe, 32 bytes of entropy from the stdlib. That is the right default for a token this system issues for itself.

It is wrong for anything with an external issuer. example-app_provider_api_key is an Anthropic key: it has to come from Anthropic. .env.example says which is which, based on the name.

docs.title: Checking what is required
docs.text:
appctl secrets check exits 1 while anything required is unset:

  example-app_provider_api_key    MISSING
  example-app_webui_token_secret  ok

1 of 4 required secrets are not set
  set them with: appctl secrets set <NAME> '<value>'
  or generate:   appctl secrets set <NAME> --generate

appctl install runs the same check before it touches the cluster and names the missing keys. Discovering a missing secret halfway through a play leaves half the guest configured.

docs.title: The documentation site
docs.text:
The repository's documentation lives next to the code it describes. That is right for GitHub: a reader lands on a file and follows relative links. It is wrong for a site, where every page has a URL and a link has to survive being moved.

scripts/build_site_docs.py is the adapter. It reads the repository's own Markdown, rewrites the links that only make sense inside a checkout, and writes the result into site_src/. MkDocs builds that tree into site/.

Neither site_src/ nor site/ is committed. The sources are the files the generator reads; the outputs are build artifacts.

docs.title: Build it locally
docs.text:
uv sync --extra docs
python scripts/build_site_docs.py --clean
uv run mkdocs build --strict --site-dir site

Serve it with a live reload while writing:

uv run python scripts/serve_docs.py

The site is served under /deployflow/ locally, because site_url names the GitHub Pages path. That prefix is not part of the site: it is where Pages will mount it.

docs.title: Why not mkdocs serve directly
docs.text:
mkdocs serve watches docs_dir, which here is site_src/ — a tree the generator writes. Editing README.md does not change site_src/, so the server never rebuilds and the browser keeps showing the old page. The watch looks broken.

scripts/serve_docs.py runs the generator, starts mkdocs serve --strict, and watches the documents the generator actually reads. A change to any of them re-runs the generator, which writes site_src/, which the server notices and rebuilds. The browser reloads a few seconds later.

It takes the address as an option: python scripts/serve_docs.py --addr 127.0.0.1:8899.

docs.title: What the generator does
docs.text:
Three kinds of link change when a document moves from the repository to the site.

In the repository On the site docs/overview.md a link to the page reference/overview.md src/appctl/cli.py an absolute URL to the file on GitHub assets/logo.png a relative path to the copied asset

The examples in that table are code spans, not links: they show what a link target looks like before and after the rewrite, and a link to a target that does not exist would be a dead link on the site.

The page map lives in PAGES in the generator: repository path → site path. Adding a document to the site means adding a row there and a line in the nav block of mkdocs.yml.

Two details are easy to get wrong.

Markdown links and raw HTML are resolved differently. MkDocs rewrites a Markdown link against the source tree. It does not touch the src and href attributes inside raw HTML, and the browser resolves those against the served URL — one directory deeper, because the page is served at <page>/. The generator emits a different relative path for each case. An image referenced with <img src="..."> that renders in the repository can be broken on the site if this is not handled.

A fenced block is copied verbatim. A link inside a code sample is an example, not a reference to follow.

docs.title: The essay
docs.text:
essay/software-delivery-needs-a-harness.md is the home page. It is a copy of the essay, kept in this repository so the site is self-contained: the site build must not depend on a file that lives somewhere else.

The essay links to the repository's own files by absolute GitHub URL. The generator rewrites those to site pages when the target is part of the site, so a reader can stay on the site, and leaves the rest as GitHub links.

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
Mermaid blocks are rendered by Material's lazy loader, which replaces a <pre class="mermaid"> element with the rendered SVG. The mermaid_fences package supplies that element — the stock superfences formatter wraps the diagram in <code>, and Mermaid cannot parse through the wrapper.

The renderer loads Mermaid from a CDN at runtime, so a diagram needs the network. Every diagram in this repository is also readable as text, which is what a reader without the CDN gets.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
The docs workflow builds the site on every change to the documentation and deploys it to the gh-pages branch on a push to main. Publishing requires the repository to have Pages enabled with the branch source set to gh-pages and the / (root) folder.

The site is at https://bruj0.github.io/deployflow.

docs.title: Delivery targets
docs.text:
A target says where and how an application runs. It is not the agent that wrote the manifest, and it is not the application.

The manifest names one:

applications:
  example-app:
    target:
      kind: proxmox_lxc
      options:
        hostname: example-app
        vmid: 121
        bind_host: 127.0.0.1

docs.title: What a target is for
docs.text:
Without the idea of a target, everything about a deployment is one thing. The tool knows about Proxmox, the roles know about Proxmox, the config knows about containers. Adding a virtual machine target then means touching all of it.

The interface separates the parts that are the same everywhere from the parts that differ:

Shared Target-specific Source and artifact Where the destination lives Configuration rendering How the destination is created or found Secret handling How the artifact is installed State recording How the application is checked The manifest schema Which checks make sense here

An application declares what it is. A target decides where it runs.

docs.title: The interface
docs.text:
Five steps, in src/appctl/targets/base.py:

class Target:
    kind: str          # what the manifest names
    summary: str       # one line, shown by `appctl targets`
    capabilities: tuple[str, ...]

    def validate(self, context): ...      # check settings and prerequisites
    def provision(self, context): ...     # create or identify the destination
    def deploy(self, context, artifacts, rendered): ...   # install and check

Each method is a step the first target actually performs. There is no method that returns "not supported", because a promise nobody keeps is worse than an absent method.

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
Called before any build, download or execution. Everything it can reject is rejected here, where nothing has happened yet:

  • a missing setting, named with the key that is missing;
  • a missing prerequisite, named with the command that would fix it;
  • an application that is not wired to a destination.

docs.title: provision
docs.text: Creates the destination or reports where it is. For proxmox_lxc the guest is created by the first play rather than here: creating it needs pct on the Proxmox host, and the play already does that, guarded by a stat so a second run is a no-op.

docs.title: deploy
docs.text: Installs the artifact, runs the application's own checks, and returns what it observed. The result carries the counts, the checks and the log directory, so the caller does not need to know how the target worked.

docs.title: The registry
docs.text:
src/appctl/targets/registry.py holds two lists:

  • implemented targets, which can be used;
  • planned targets, which cannot.
registry.resolve("proxmox_lxc")   # returns the target
registry.resolve("vm")            # TargetError: planned but not implemented
registry.resolve("mainframe")     # TargetError: unknown target kind

The resolution never falls back. An application that asks for a virtual machine must not be silently installed into a container, and the only way to guarantee that is to fail.

docs.title: The implemented target: proxmox_lxc
docs.text:
Everything Proxmox-specific lives in src/appctl/targets/proxmox_lxc.py:

  • the container ID and the guest hostname;
  • the template, the storage, the bridge and the guest network;
  • the pct operations that create the guest and discover its DHCP lease;
  • the SSH connection to the guest.

The shared code above it knows none of them.

docs.title: Writing a target
docs.text:
The interface is small enough that a new target is a single file. It has to answer four questions honestly:

  1. What are its settings? They go in target.options. The shared schema does not read inside them, so a new target never changes config.py.
  2. What must be true before it runs? validate checks it and says what is wrong.
  3. How does it install the artifact? deploy does it, using the same rendered configuration and the same secret values as every other target.
  4. What proves the application works? The application's own checks, plus whatever the target adds.

docs.title: What a target must not do
docs.text:
• It must not decide what to install. It receives a built artifact and hands it over.
  • It must not weaken a check. A target that cannot run an application's checks has to say so, not skip them.
  • It must not pretend. A target that implements part of an operation should implement the whole of it or not claim it.

docs.title: The planned targets
docs.text: Neither is implemented. Both are named in the registry so that a manifest can name them and get a clear answer.

docs.title: vm
docs.text:
Would provision a virtual machine and install the application into it.

It would need: machine creation or selection, boot and address discovery, guest access, and a way to install an artifact that is not a wheel. It would also need its own checks, because "the VM is running" is not "the application works".

docs.title: docker_vm
docs.text:
Would provision a virtual machine and run the application in Docker there.

It would need everything vm needs, plus: Docker availability on the guest, image provenance, runtime configuration, ports and volumes, and container health. A container that starts is not an application that answers.

docs.title: What each would have to prove
docs.text:
A planned target becomes supported when:

  • the same application intent installs on it and on proxmox_lxc;
  • the application's own checks pass there;
  • a second install reports no change;
  • one deliberate failure is caught by a check, not by a red play.

Until then it stays in the planned list. The README says the same thing, so a reader is not misled.
